Comparisons: 82 “X vs Y” pairs

Each pair has the slide table, the one-line key difference (yellow) and the scenario cue that tells you which side a question means. “High” pairs are on the slides as an explicit comparison or asked in the pool; they come first.

Week
Likely

Hadoop 1.x (JobTracker) vs Hadoop 2.x (YARN)Week 5 · P1 s7, s9; P2 s4, s6, s12; P1 s29 (MCQ Q4)

high
Hadoop 1.x (JobTracker)Hadoop 2.x (YARN)
DesignJobTracker = resource mgmt + job scheduling in one monolithResourceManager (global scheduler) separated from per-job ApplicationMaster
Max nodes~4,000>10,000
FrameworksMR onlyAny (Spark, Tez, Samza ...)
Resource unitSlot (fixed)Container (flexible)
AMIn JobTrackerPer-app process
RM HANoYes (ZooKeeper)
Key differenceHadoop 1.x's single JobTracker mixed resource management with MapReduce job scheduling (MapReduce only, ~4,000-node ceiling); YARN (Hadoop 2.0, 2013) split this into a global ResourceManager and a per-job ApplicationMaster, so any framework can share a 10,000+ node cluster.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a cluster that can only run MapReduce, stalls near 4,000 nodes, or one daemon doing both scheduling and job tracking, the answer is Hadoop 1.x / JobTracker; if Spark, Tez and MapReduce share one cluster, it is YARN.
Card: YARN and its three components →

ResourceManager (RM) vs ApplicationMaster (AM)Week 5 · P1 s10-11; P2 s7, s11; P1 s28 (MCQ Q1 note)

high
ResourceManager (RM)ApplicationMaster (AM)
How manyOne per cluster, on a dedicated master nodeOne per running job (application)
RoleGlobal cluster resource schedulerThe job's own scheduler
Parts / dutiesScheduler (allocates containers; FIFO/Fair/Capacity) + ApplicationsManager (accepts jobs, starts first container for each AM)Requests containers from RM, tells NM to launch tasks, monitors progress, re-requests for failed tasks, releases containers
Framework knowledgeFramework-agnosticHolds the framework-specific logic (MR AM, Spark AM, Tez AM, Samza AM)
If it failsYARN 2.4+: ZooKeeper Active/Standby RM, failover < 60 sRM restarts the AM (max attempts, default 2)
Slide exampleGrants 80 containers (cluster busy)Spark AM requests 100 containers (4 cores, 8 GB each)
Key differenceThe ResourceManager is the single global scheduler that hands out containers for the whole cluster, while an ApplicationMaster is a per-job process that negotiates containers from the RM and runs that one job's tasks.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question says 'one per cluster / decides which application gets which containers', the answer is the ResourceManager; if it says 'one per job / requests containers on behalf of the job / restarts failed tasks', it is the ApplicationMaster.
Card: YARN and its three components →

NodeManager failure vs ApplicationMaster failureWeek 5 · P2 s11; P1 s12; P1 s32 (A2)

high
NodeManager failureApplicationMaster failure
Detected byRM, via missing heartbeat (>10 min)RM
State changeAll containers on that node marked failedAM attempt counted (yarn.resourcemanager.am.max-attempts, default 2)
RecoveryAM is notified and re-requests containers elsewhereRM restarts a new AM
Job stateTasks re-run in new containersNew AM recovers state from HDFS checkpoints if the framework supports it (MapReduce: yes; early Spark: no)
Third case (RM failure)-YARN 2.4+: ZooKeeper promotes Standby RM in < 60 s
Key differenceA NodeManager failure is caught by the RM through missed heartbeats and the job's AM re-requests the lost containers elsewhere, whereas an AM failure is handled by the RM restarting the AM itself (default 2 attempts), recovering state from HDFS checkpoints if supported.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question traces a worker node (e.g. NM2 with 5 containers) dying mid-job, the answer is the NodeManager-failure path (heartbeat timeout -> containers failed -> AM re-requests); if the job's coordinator dies, it is the AM-restart path.
Card: YARN fault tolerance →

Capacity Scheduler vs Fair SchedulerWeek 5 · P1 s13-14; P2 s10, s17, s21

high
Capacity SchedulerFair Scheduler
PolicyCluster divided into queues with guaranteed capacity; elastically borrows unused capacityAll jobs get equal share of resources
Slide exampleEngineering 60% / Finance 40%; a2i queues 60/30/10; LinkedIn 6 queues (production 40%)Latency-sensitive short jobs complete quickly even if a large job is running
Default in / used byHDP/CDH; Yahoo!, LinkedInCloudera; Facebook, Twitter
StrengthSLAs: production queue guaranteed minimum; adhoc queries cannot starve revenue pipelinesSmall jobs get fast turnaround
Contrast with FIFOFIFO: one queue, submission order; one long job starves all othersFIFO not suitable for multi-tenant clusters
Key differenceThe Capacity Scheduler gives each team's queue a guaranteed percentage of the cluster (lending idle capacity), whereas the Fair Scheduler shares resources equally among running jobs so short jobs finish fast; FIFO simply runs jobs in submission order and lets one long job starve the rest.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes several teams/departments that each need a guaranteed share (e.g. 60% health batch, 30% streaming, 10% ad hoc), the answer is the Capacity Scheduler; if many short interactive jobs must not wait behind a big one, it is the Fair Scheduler; a single queue in arrival order is FIFO.
Card: Schedulers and capacity planning →

Row store (CSV / JSON / Avro) vs Columnar store (Parquet / ORC)Week 5 · P1 s6, s16, s17, s22-23; P1 s30 (T/F 1), s31 (D2)

high
Row store (CSV / JSON / Avro)Columnar store (Parquet / ORC)
Layout on diskRecord by record (id, name, age, score together)Column by column
SELECT score FROM usersReads ALL columnsReads ONLY the score column
100-col, 10 TB table, 3-col queryCSV reads all 10 TBParquet reads ~300 GB (33x speedup; 97% I/O reduction)
Filter skippingNoneMin/max stats per row group -> predicate pushdown skips row groups
Best forPortability, small data; row-append streaming ingest (Avro)Analytical, read-heavy workloads (Spark, Presto, ML, Hive)
Key differenceA row store keeps each record's fields together so any query reads every column, while a columnar store keeps each column together so a query reads only the columns it needs (3 of 100 columns -> ~3% of the data).
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes an analyst query that touches a few columns of a very wide table and is slow on CSV, the answer is to switch to columnar (Parquet/ORC); if it describes appending whole events or exchanging records, a row format (Avro/CSV) fits.
Card: Row vs columnar storage and Parquet →

Avro vs ParquetWeek 5 · P1 s17-18, s21, s25-26; P1 s31 (D3)

high
AvroParquet
OrientationRowColumnar
SchemaSelf-describing (JSON); reader vs writer schemaSelf-describing
Key strengthSchema evolution: missing fields use defaults, extra fields ignored (backward + forward compatible)Row groups (~128 MB) with min/max stats -> predicate pushdown
CodecSnappy / DeflateSnappy / Gzip
Best forStreaming ingest Kafka -> HDFS; data exchangeSpark analytics, Presto, ML pipelines
bKash strategyIngest layer (API versioning)Analytics layer, converted nightly (Parquet+Snappy)
Key differenceAvro is a row-oriented format whose reader/writer schema handles schema evolution, so it suits append-heavy streaming ingest, whereas Parquet is columnar with per-row-group statistics, so it suits analytic reads that select few columns and filter.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes LinkedIn adding a new field to Kafka events without breaking old consumers, the answer is Avro; if it describes analysts running Spark/Presto queries over a few columns, it is Parquet.
Card: File formats: Avro, Parquet, ORC →

Splittable (Parquet+Snappy, bzip2, LZO+index) vs Not splittable (Gzip CSV)Week 5 · P1 s20-21, s25, s29 (MCQ Q3), s30 (T/F 3), s32 (A1)

high
Splittable (Parquet+Snappy, bzip2, LZO+index)Not splittable (Gzip CSV)
DefinitionHDFS can start reading from any point in the file without decompressing from the beginningMust decompress from the beginning
10 GB fileMultiple Mappers process different parts simultaneously (e.g. 3 row groups -> 3 Mappers)Exactly 1 Mapper - no parallelism
WhyParquet splits at row-group boundaries; bzip2 natively splittableMapReduce cannot split across gzip boundaries even though HDFS stores it in blocks
BenefitEnables data-local task scheduling-
Slide verdictBest practice: Parquet + Snappy for analytics'The Gzip Trap - very common mistake'; avoid raw gzip on large CSV
Key differenceA splittable file can be read from any point so many Mappers work on it in parallel, whereas a gzip-compressed CSV must be decompressed from the start, so one Mapper reads the whole file.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a big gzip CSV processed by a single slow Mapper (e.g. telecom CDRs taking 6 hours), the answer is 'not splittable - convert to Parquet+Snappy (or bzip2)'.
Card: Compression codecs and splittability →

Snappy vs GzipWeek 5 · P1 s20, s25

high
SnappyGzip
SpeedFastSlow
RatioMediumHigh
Splittable?No (but Parquet row groups are)No
Matrix useAvro ingest; Parquet Spark analyticsParquet ML features
Other codecsLZO: fast/medium, splittable with index; Zstd: fast/high, block-levelBzip2: slowest/highest, splittable; ORC + Zlib for Hive warehouse
Key differenceSnappy trades a medium compression ratio for high speed, whereas Gzip compresses more but slowly; neither is splittable on raw files, so both are used inside splittable containers like Parquet.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks for a codec for a speed-critical Spark analytics or Kafka ingest pipeline, the answer is Snappy; for storage-heavy ML feature files it lists Gzip; for cold archive, Zstd; if splittability on a raw file is required, bzip2 or LZO+index.
Card: Compression codecs and splittability →

MapReduce vs SparkWeek 6 · P1 s6-7, s31-32; P2 s4-5, s10, s16; P1 s34, s36

high
MapReduceSpark
Intermediate storageDisk (HDFS) after every stepMemory (spill to disk if needed)
Iterative algorithmsSlow (disk per iteration); K-Means 100 iters = 10 TB I/OFast (cache RDD; 10-100x); 50 GB read once
Fault toleranceRe-execute task from HDFSRecompute from lineage
Programming model / languagesMap + Reduce only; Javamap, filter, join, groupBy, SQL, ML, stream; Python, Scala, Java, R
Streaming / interactiveNot supported natively; not feasible (>30 s)Structured Streaming; Spark Shell (sub-second)
Use whenSingle-pass batch where Spark's ~8 GB/Executor overhead is prohibitive, or stable MR codeML, graph, interactive, streaming, >2 iterations over same data
Key differenceMapReduce writes every intermediate result to HDFS, so iterative jobs pay disk I/O on every pass, whereas Spark caches the working set in memory as RDDs and recovers from lineage, making iterative work 10-100x faster.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes an ML or graph job that loops many times over the same data (K-Means, logistic regression, PageRank), the answer is Spark; a one-pass batch job on a huge cluster with tight memory can stay on MapReduce.
Card: Why Spark: the MapReduce iteration bottleneck →

HDFS replication (traditional) vs RDD lineage (Spark)Week 6 · P1 s13-15; P2 s7-8, s16, s20; P1 s34 (MCQ Q2), s37 (D1)

high
HDFS replication (traditional)RDD lineage (Spark)
What is kept3 copies of the dataThe computation graph (log of transformations)
Recovering a lost partitionRead another copyRe-read the HDFS input for that partition and re-apply the same transformations
OverheadReplication overheadNo data replication overhead - 'the computation is the backup'
Weak spot-Expensive for wide dependencies (many ancestors); checkpoint long chains to HDFS
Slide lesson-Recomputing from lineage is cheaper than maintaining 3x replicated in-memory state
Key differenceHDFS tolerates failures by storing three copies of the data, whereas an RDD stores only how it was derived and recomputes a lost partition from its parents, so there is no replication overhead.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks how Spark recovers a lost partition without copying data (e.g. an executor holding partitions 3 and 7 crashes), the answer is lineage recomputation; for HDFS block loss, it is replication.
Card: RDDs and lineage-based fault tolerance →

Transformation vs ActionWeek 6 · P1 s17-20; P2 s8; P1 s35 (MCQ Q4), s37 (D2, D3)

high
TransformationAction
EvaluationLazy: builds the DAG, does not executeEager: triggers execution of the DAG
ReturnsA new RDDA value to the Driver, or writes to storage
Examplesmap, filter, flatMap, distinct, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, cachecollect, count, first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach
RuleNo transformation executes until an action is calledSpark then analyses the full DAG, pipelines, runs only needed partitions
Slide examplerdd.filter(x > 1000) records only.first() stops after the first match
Key differenceA transformation lazily defines a new RDD and only adds to the DAG, while an action forces the DAG to run and returns a value to the Driver or writes output.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question shows a chain like filter().map() and asks why nothing ran, the answer is that these are lazy transformations; the first count()/collect()/saveAsTextFile() is the action that triggers the job.
Card: Transformations, actions and lazy evaluation →

Narrow dependency vs Wide dependencyWeek 6 · P1 s14, s21-22; P2 s9, s16, s20

high
Narrow dependencyWide dependency
Partition mappingEach output partition depends on at most one input partition (1-to-1)Each output partition may depend on multiple input partitions (all-to-all)
Examplesmap, filter, flatMap, union, mapPartitions, coalescegroupByKey, reduceByKey, aggregateByKey, join (not co-partitioned), repartition, distinct, sortByKey
Data movementNo shuffleShuffle across the network
StagesPipelined within a single stageCreates a stage boundary
RecoveryRecompute only that partition from its single parentMust recompute from all parent partitions (expensive)
Key differenceIn a narrow dependency each child partition needs at most one parent partition, so it pipelines in one stage with no shuffle, whereas a wide dependency needs many parent partitions, forcing a network shuffle and a new stage.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question shows a DAG and asks where the stage boundary is, put it at the first wide operation (reduceByKey, groupByKey, join, repartition); map/filter chains stay in one stage.
Card: Narrow vs wide dependencies, stages and shuffle →

reduceByKey vs groupByKeyWeek 6 · P1 s22; P2 s18 (live exercise Q3)

high
reduceByKeygroupByKey
DependencyWide (shuffle)Wide (shuffle)
Before shufflingApplies a local combine (like a MapReduce Combiner)Ships all values per key
Network trafficGreatly reducedLarger
Slide advicePrefer reduceByKeyAvoid when an aggregate is all you need (inference from 'prefer reduceByKey')
How to checkSpark UI (localhost:4040) shuffle read/write bytes - smallerShuffle read/write bytes - larger
Key differenceBoth shuffle, but reduceByKey pre-aggregates values on each partition before the shuffle (like a Combiner), so far less data crosses the network than with groupByKey.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a word count or per-key sum that is slow because of heavy shuffle, the answer is to replace groupByKey with reduceByKey.

DataFrame vs RDDWeek 6 · P1 s26, s36 (T/F 3); P2 s11, s20

high
DataFrameRDD
StructureDistributed collection organised into named columns with a schemaRead-only partitioned collection of records
OptimiserCatalyst (predicate pushdown, join reordering, constant folding)DAG scheduler only
Speed (structured data)10-100x faster than RDDsBaseline
APISQL syntax + Python/Scala method chainingFunctional: map, filter, lambdas
Use whenDefault for structured dataLow-level control needed
RelationshipBuilt on top of RDDs; compiles down to an RDD planRDDs largely replaced by DataFrames/Datasets since Spark 2.0
Key differenceA DataFrame adds named columns and a schema so the Catalyst optimiser can rewrite the query before running it (10-100x faster on structured data), whereas an RDD is schema-less records processed with functional operators.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes structured tabular data queried with SQL/aggregations, the answer is DataFrame/Spark SQL; if it needs custom low-level per-record control, RDD.

Schema-on-write (RDBMS / MySQL) vs Schema-on-read (Hive)Week 7 · P1 s13-14; P1 s28 (MCQ Q2), s31 (D3); P2 s6-7

high
Schema-on-write (RDBMS / MySQL)Schema-on-read (Hive)
When schema enforcedAt INSERT / LOAD timeAt SELECT / query time
Invalid dataRejected immediately (INSERT fails if amount is text)Stored; NULL returned at query ('abc' in amount -> NULL)
Write speed / query speedSlower write (validation); faster queryFast write (raw file copy); slower query (parse per query)
Schemas per dataOne schema per tableMany schemas on same data
Storage formatProprietary (InnoDB pages)Open: ORC, Parquet, CSV, JSON, Avro
Use caseOLTP: e-commerce orders, bankingOLAP: log analysis, batch reporting
Key differenceSchema-on-write validates data against the table schema when it is loaded and rejects bad rows, while schema-on-read stores raw files as-is and applies the schema only when queried, so bad values silently become NULL.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes loading raw web logs immediately and defining several tables over them later, or a corrupt column quietly returning NULL, the answer is schema-on-read; if an INSERT is rejected for a type error, it is schema-on-write.
Card: Schema-on-read and HiveQL vs SQL →

SQL (RDBMS) vs HiveQLWeek 7 · P1 s16-17; P1 s30 (T/F 1)

high
SQL (RDBMS)HiveQL
ACID / UPDATE / DELETEFull; any row, any timeLimited: only ORC tables in ACID (transactional) mode
IndexingB-tree, hash, bitmapPartitions + buckets (no traditional indexes)
Sub-queriesCorrelatedNon-correlated only (some limitations)
LatencyMillisecondsMinutes (MapReduce) / seconds (Tez/Spark)
Execution / data locationSingle-node or MPP; database storage engineDistributed MR/Tez/Spark DAG; HDFS directories
Scale / workloadTerabytes max; OLTPPetabytes; OLAP
Key differenceHiveQL looks like SQL but compiles to distributed batch jobs over HDFS, so it scales to petabytes yet has minute-level latency, limited ACID/UPDATE and no traditional indexes, unlike an RDBMS's millisecond OLTP SQL.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question expects millisecond response or row-level UPDATEs from Hive, the answer is the misconception 'HiveQL = SQL'; a COUNT(*) on 1 TB can take 5-10 minutes - use Presto or Spark SQL for interactive latency.

Partitioning vs BucketingWeek 7 · P1 s19-24; P1 s29 (MCQ Q3 note), s30 (T/F 2, 4), s31 (D2), s32 (A1)

high
PartitioningBucketing
Physical unitSeparate HDFS sub-directory per column value (year=2024/month=01/)Fixed number of files (buckets) inside each partition
Decided byValue of the partition columnhash(column) % N
Main benefitPartition pruning: skips non-matching directories, avoids full-table scanBucket map join: bucket i x bucket i, no full sort-merge shuffle
Good columnLow-cardinality, used in WHERE (date, country, region, status)The join key, e.g. user_id (slide example; 'high-cardinality' is general knowledge)
RiskHigh-cardinality key -> partition explosion (100 M directories crash NameNode)Both tables must use same key and same bucket count
DDLPARTITIONED BY (year INT, month INT)CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS
Key differencePartitioning splits a table into directories by a low-cardinality column value so WHERE filters skip whole directories, while bucketing hashes a (high-cardinality) column into a fixed number of files so tables bucketed the same way can be joined bucket-to-bucket without a full shuffle.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes daily reports filtered by country and date, the answer is partition on (country/date); if it describes repeatedly joining with a 10 M-row user table on user_id, bucket on user_id - often both together.
Card: Bucketing and bucket map join →

Hive (+MapReduce) vs Presto / TrinoWeek 7 · P1 s6, s17, s26; P1 s29 (MCQ Q4 note); P2 s4

high
Hive (+MapReduce)Presto / Trino
OriginFacebook, 2008Meta (Facebook), 2013
Execution modelCompiled to MR / Tez / Spark jobsIn-memory pipeline execution (split -> stage -> output)
Intermediate resultsMaterialised to HDFS between every MapReduce stageNo intermediate disk writes
Latency5-15 min (minutes)5-60 sec (seconds); '10x faster than Hive+MapReduce'
OptimisationsPartition pruning, bucketingVectorized execution (1,024-row batches), cost-based optimizer, connector architecture (HDFS, Hive, Cassandra, MySQL, Kafka, S3 in one query)

Point-to-point ETL vs Event-driven pipeline (message bus)Week 8 · P1 s5-6, s14

high
Point-to-point ETLEvent-driven pipeline (message bus)
ConnectionsO(N^2): at 50 systems ~2,450 ETL jobsEach source publishes once to a central bus; consumers subscribe
Schema changeBrittle: breaks its ETL jobsDecoupled
ReplayNone: offline consumer loses dataReplayable from the retained log
LatencyNightly batch, >= 24 hoursReal time
Adding a consumerNew jobs, tightly bound to sourceZero changes to any source system
Key differencePoint-to-point ETL wires every pair of systems directly (O(N^2) brittle nightly jobs, no replay), whereas an event-driven pipeline routes everything through one bus like Kafka, so sources and consumers are decoupled, real-time and replayable.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes 50 systems with thousands of fragile nightly ETL jobs that break on every schema change, the answer is to replace them with a central Kafka event bus.

high
SqoopFlume

ThroughputGB-TB/hourMB-GB/hour

Flume vs KafkaWeek 8 · P1 s7, s12, s14, s19; P2 s12

high
FlumeKafka
PurposeOptimised for log collection to HDFSGeneral-purpose event bus
DirectionLogs -> HDFSAny -> Any
ModeBatch / micro-batchReal-time stream
Durability / replayFile channel survives agent crash; no replay (inference: slide credits Kafka with the stronger durability and replay)Stronger durability and replay from any offset
TodayOften replaced by Kafka producers writing directly from applicationsKafka Connect replaces Sqoop and Flume for most use cases

Traditional queue vs Kafka append-only logWeek 8 · P1 s14-15; P2 s5; P1 s32 (MCQ Q2), s34 (T/F 2)

high
Traditional queueKafka append-only log
After a message is consumedDeletedRetained for a configured period (days, weeks, or forever)
Late-joining consumerMisses dataReads from offset 0 and replays the entire history
Who tracks read positionBroker (inference from 'the Kafka broker never tracks what a consumer has read')Consumer tracks its own offset; broker never tracks it
Many consumers-Each consumer (group) reads independently at its own offset
Benefit-New pipelines built without re-ingesting from source
Key differenceA traditional queue deletes a message once consumed and the broker tracks delivery, whereas Kafka keeps an append-only log for a retention period and each consumer tracks its own offset, so late or new consumers can replay history.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a new analytics team that needs last week's events without re-ingesting from the source database, the answer is Kafka's retained log (start at offset 0).

Kafka vs ActiveMQ / RabbitMQ (traditional MOM)Week 8 · P2 s4, s9, s11, s22

high
KafkaActiveMQ / RabbitMQ (traditional MOM)
Designed forSustained 100 MB/s per broker, multi-day retention, replayTransactional messaging: few thousand msgs/sec, guaranteed delivery, complex routing
Producer throughput (paper)50.5 MB/s (505,000 msgs/s)ActiveMQ 4.3 MB/s; RabbitMQ 14.7 MB/s
Consumer throughput22.0 MB/sActiveMQ 4.0; RabbitMQ 8.2 MB/s
AcknowledgementPer batchPer message
Data pathSequential writes + zero-copy sendfile() (2 copies)Disk -> kernel -> user space -> socket -> NIC (4 copies)
ConsumersPull; one log serves all consumersPer-consumer queues
Key differenceActiveMQ and RabbitMQ were built for low-volume transactional messaging with per-message acknowledgements, whereas Kafka uses sequential append-only logs, zero-copy, batching and consumer pull to reach ~10x their throughput with retention and replay.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks why LinkedIn could not use ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ for billions of activity events per day, the answer: they targeted a few thousand msgs/sec without retention or replay; Kafka reached 50.5 MB/s vs 4.3/14.7.

Lambda (Marz, 2011) vs Kappa (Kreps, 2014)Week 8 · P1 s21-27; P1 s33 (MCQ Q4), s34 (T/F 3), s35 (D1), s36 (A2); P2 s15, s18

high
Lambda (Marz, 2011)Kappa (Kreps, 2014)
Code pathsTwo (batch + stream) - must stay in syncOne (stream only)
Historical reprocessingRe-run batch job on HDFSReplay Kafka log from offset 0
LatencyLow (speed layer) + high (batch layer)Low throughout
ComplexityHigh: two systems, merging layer; 30-40% of effort keeping layers consistentLower: single pipeline
Batch throughput / storageVery high (Spark/Hive on full dataset); HDFS master datasetLimited by stream engine; Kafka (bounded) + S3/Iceberg
Use whenLogic too complex for stream-only; batch ML training; regulatory batch reportsStream engine fast enough to reprocess; single code path worth the stream-storage cost
Key differenceLambda runs a batch layer and a speed layer with the same logic implemented twice and merges them in a serving layer, whereas Kappa drops the batch layer and uses one stream-processing code path, reprocessing history by replaying the Kafka log from offset 0.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question describes a team tired of maintaining the same logic in Spark batch and Spark Streaming, the answer is Kappa; if a regulator mandates separate batch reconciliation or TB+ history is too slow to replay, keep Lambda.

Batch layer vs Speed layerWeek 8 · P1 s21-23, s33 (MCQ Q3 note); P2 s15-16

high
Batch layerSpeed layer
Data handledComplete, immutable master dataset (HDFS); periodically recomputes batch viewsNew data arriving since the last batch job
ToolsHDFS + Spark/Hive (hourly or nightly)Kafka + Spark Streaming / Flink
OutputAccurateApproximate
LatencyHigh: 1-24 hours staleLow: < seconds
NetflixKafka -> S3 -> Spark + Iceberg, ~1 day (ML training, billing)Kafka -> Flink, < 1 minute (dashboards, alerts, A/B counters)
Serving layer (not a processing layer)Query = batch view (up to N hours ago)UNION real-time view (last N hours)
Key differenceThe batch layer periodically recomputes accurate views from the full immutable master dataset (hours stale), while the speed layer processes only recent data with a stream engine to give approximate results within seconds; the serving layer merges the two.
Spot it in a scenarioIf the question asks which Lambda layer gives real-time low-latency views, the answer is the speed layer (not the serving layer, which only merges and serves).

Data lake vs Data warehouseWeek 8 · P1 s29-30, s35 (D3); W07 P1 s13; W07 P2 s4

Key differenceThe Hive Metastore is a relational DB holding table schemas, partitions and SerDe information, whereas the NameNode holds only HDFS block metadata; the NameNode is the common distractor for 'where is Hive schema stored'.

Slide problems: 69 worked examples

The teacher said solving the slide exercises covers the paper. Each problem shows the slide's given numbers; tap for the worked steps. Then do the two one-step variants and the “why” question, and mark each Known or Again.

Week
Rank

Analytical A1: telecom CDR, 10 TB gzip CSV, 4 of 80 columns, 6 hoursWeek 5 · W05 P1 s32 (Analytical A1)

very likely
Given10 TB daily CDR on HDFS as gzip CSV. A Hive query selects 4 of 80 columns and takes 6 hours. Several teams share the cluster.
Worked solution · 7 steps (tap)
  1. Reason 1: CSV is a row store, so all 80 columns are read for a 4-column query.
  2. Reason 2: gzip is not splittable, so each file is read by one Mapper (little parallelism).
  3. Migration: Parquet (or ORC for Hive) + Snappy, partitioned by call date (and region).
  4. Column pruning alone: read 4/80 = 5% of the data = 10 TB x 4/80 = 500 GB.
  5. I/O reduction = 1 - 4/80 = 95%, speedup about 80/4 = 20x.
  6. If the job is I/O-bound: 6 h / 20 = 18 min, before any gain from partition pruning or splittable parallelism.
  7. Scheduler: Capacity (guaranteed queue per team, elastic borrowing) or Fair.
AnswerRead 500 GB instead of 10 TB (95% less, 20x); about 18 min if I/O bound; Capacity Scheduler for multi-team sharing.
Practice · 3
Same company, new query reads 8 of 80 columns. Given: Parquet reads D x k/N. How much of the 10 TB does it read?
Variant 1
10 TB x 8/80 = 1 TB.
After the move to Parquet, the 4-column query reads 500 GB. The table is also partitioned by day and the query asks for 1 of 30 days. How much is read now?
Variant 2
500 GB / 30 = 16.7 GB.
Why are both format and codec to blame, not just one?
Why
The format (row CSV) makes every query read all 80 columns. The codec (gzip) blocks splitting, so even that oversized read happens in very few Mappers. Fixing only one leaves the other cost: Parquet + gzip stays splittable at row groups, but CSV + Snappy still reads every column.
Card: Row vs columnar storage and Parquet →

Analytical A2: NodeManager NM2 with 5 containers failsWeek 5 · W05 P1 s12, s32 (Analytical A2); W05 P2 s11

very likely
GivenNM2 hosts 5 running containers of a MapReduce job and fails mid-run. RM marks a node lost after missed heartbeats (paper: >10 min). AM max attempts default 2. RM HA failover < 60 s.
Worked solution · 6 steps (tap)
  1. NM2 stops sending heartbeats to the RM.
  2. After the expiry interval (>10 min) the RM marks NM2 lost and all 5 of its containers FAILED; it removes NM2's capacity from the scheduler.
  3. The RM tells the job's AM that those 5 containers are gone.
  4. The AM re-requests 5 replacement containers from the RM.
  5. The RM grants containers on healthy nodes; the AM tells those NMs to launch the 5 tasks again (general knowledge: completed map output on NM2 is also re-run if reducers still need it).
  6. If the AM itself had been on NM2, the RM would restart the AM (up to 2 attempts) and MapReduce recovers job state from HDFS.
AnswerDetection by RM heartbeat timeout; RM marks 5 containers failed; AM re-requests 5 containers; tasks rerun on other NMs.
Practice · 3
An AM restart limit is 2 attempts. The AM crashes once, restarts, then crashes again. Given: the RM restarts the AM up to max-attempts. Does the job survive?
Variant 1
No. Two attempts are used (original + 1 restart = 2), so on the second failure the job fails.
A node hosting 8 containers, each {4 GB, 2 vCPU}, is lost. How much capacity does the AM need to re-request?
Variant 2
8 x 4 = 32 GB and 8 x 2 = 16 vCPU.
Why does the AM, not the RM, restart the failed tasks?
Why
The RM only knows containers, not what ran inside them. Task-level recovery (which tasks, which input split, whether output must be redone) is framework logic, which YARN delegates to each job's AM.
Card: YARN fault tolerance →

ApplicationMaster asks for 100 containers, RM grants 80Week 5 · W05 P1 s11

very likely
GivenA Spark AM requests 100 containers, each 4 cores and 8 GB RAM. The cluster is busy; the RM grants 80.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Requested: 100 x 4 = 400 cores, 100 x 8 = 800 GB.
  2. Granted: 80 x 4 = 320 cores, 80 x 8 = 640 GB.
  3. Shortfall: 20 containers = 20% of the request (80 cores, 160 GB).
  4. The AM assigns tasks to the 80 executors it has and keeps asking for more as resources free up.
Answer80 executors with 320 cores and 640 GB; the job runs at 80% of the parallelism it asked for.
Practice · 3
A MapReduce AM asks for 50 containers of {2 vCPU, 4 GB}. The RM grants 35. Given: granted resources = containers x size. How much RAM does the job hold?
Variant 1
35 x 4 GB = 140 GB (and 35 x 2 = 70 vCPU).
Granted 35 of 50 containers. Each task takes 10 min and there are 350 tasks. How many waves of tasks run, and how long does it take?
Variant 2
350 / 35 = 10 waves x 10 min = 100 min (with all 50 it would be 7 waves = 70 min).
Why does the AM, not the ResourceManager, decide which task runs in which container?
Why
The RM is a global, framework-agnostic scheduler: it only hands out resource slices. Task placement, retries and progress are framework-specific, so they live in the per-job AM. This split is what lets Spark, MapReduce and Tez share one YARN cluster.
Card: YARN and its three components →

Columnar storage: 3 of 100 columns from 10 TB (97% less I/O, 33x)Week 5 · W05 P1 s6, s16

very likely
GivenA 100-column table holds 10 TB. A query selects 3 columns. CSV (row store) vs Parquet (column store).
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Row store (CSV) must read every column of every row: 10 TB.
  2. Column store reads only the 3 needed columns: 10 TB x 3/100 = 0.3 TB = 300 GB (assumes columns of equal size).
  3. I/O reduction = 1 - 3/100 = 97%.
  4. Speedup from format alone = 100/3 = 33.33x, which the slide rounds to 33x.
AnswerParquet reads about 300 GB instead of 10 TB: 97% less I/O, about 33x faster.
Practice · 3
A telecom keeps a 200-column, 20 TB call-record table. An analyst's query uses 5 columns. Given: a column store reads D x k/N. How much data does Parquet read?
Variant 1
20 TB x 5/200 = 0.5 TB = 500 GB.
Same 200-column table, 5 columns read. Parquet reads 500 GB of the 20 TB. State the I/O reduction and the speedup.
Variant 2
Reduction = 1 - 5/200 = 97.5%; speedup = 200/5 = 40x.
Why does a columnar file read less data for SELECT score FROM users, and when would it not help?
Why
Each column is stored contiguously, so the reader seeks to the score column chunk and physically skips id, name and age on disk. A row store interleaves all columns, so every byte must be read. It does not help when the query needs all or most columns (SELECT *), or for row-at-a-time writes.
Card: Row vs columnar storage and Parquet →

The gzip trap: a 10 GB gzip CSV gets exactly 1 MapperWeek 5 · W05 P1 s20-s21, s25

very likely
GivenA 10 GB gzip-compressed CSV on HDFS. Gzip is not splittable. Parquet row groups are about 128 MB and are splittable.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Gzip has no internal block boundaries; a reader must decompress from the start.
  2. So MapReduce cannot start a second Mapper mid-file: 1 Mapper reads all 10 GB, no parallelism.
  3. Same data as Parquet + Snappy, row groups about 128 MB: 10 x 1,024 MB / 128 MB = 80 row groups.
  4. Each row group is one split, so up to 80 Mappers can run in parallel.
AnswerGzip: 1 Mapper. Parquet with 128 MB row groups: about 80 parallel Mappers.
Practice · 3
A 2 GB bzip2 file on HDFS with 128 MB blocks. Bzip2 is splittable. How many Mappers?
Variant 1
2 x 1,024 / 128 = 16 Mappers.
A 6.4 GB file: one copy is gzip, one is LZO with an index. Block 128 MB. Mappers for each?
Variant 2
Gzip: 1 (not splittable). LZO with index: 6.4 x 1,024 / 128 = 51.2, so about 52 Mappers.
HDFS already stores the gzip file in blocks. Why can't each block get its own Mapper?
Why
Blocks split the bytes, not the compressed stream. A gzip stream can only be decoded from its beginning, so a Mapper given block 5 cannot decompress it without first decoding blocks 1-4. The fix is Parquet + Snappy (splittable at row groups) or bzip2 (natively splittable). The matrix marks CSV + Gzip as AVOID.
Card: Compression codecs and splittability →

Live Exercise: YARN capacity planning on LinkedIn's 5,000-node clusterWeek 5 · W05 P2 s23-s25 (Live Exercise)

very likely
Given5,000 nodes, each 64 GB RAM and 16 vCPU. Capacity Scheduler: production 40%, spark 25%, samza 15%, adhoc 10%, reserve 10%. Containers: Hive mapper {4 GB, 2 vCPU} (production and adhoc), Spark executor {8 GB, 4 vCPU}, Samza task {2 GB, 1 vCPU}.
Worked solution · 6 steps (tap)
  1. production: nodes 2,000, RAM 128,000 GB, vCPU 32,000; by RAM 32,000, by CPU 16,000; max 16,000 (CPU bound).
  2. spark: nodes 1,250, RAM 80,000 GB, vCPU 20,000; by RAM 10,000, by CPU 5,000; max 5,000 (CPU bound).
  3. samza: nodes 750, RAM 48,000 GB, vCPU 12,000; by RAM 24,000, by CPU 12,000; max 12,000 (CPU bound).
  4. adhoc: nodes 500, RAM 32,000 GB, vCPU 8,000; by RAM 8,000, by CPU 4,000; max 4,000 (CPU bound).
  5. Q2: every container asks 2 GB per vCPU but a node has 64/16 = 4 GB per vCPU, so CPU runs out first everywhere; half the RAM sits idle.
  6. Q3: per node min(64/4, 16/2) = 8 Hive mappers; 10,000 / 8 = 1,250 nodes (production owns 2,000, so it fits).
AnswerMax containers: production 16,000, spark 5,000, samza 12,000, adhoc 4,000. Bottleneck: CPU. 10,000 Hive mappers need 1,250 nodes.
Practice · 3
Spark queue: 1,250 nodes, so 80,000 GB and 20,000 vCPU (given). Executors are {8 GB, 4 vCPU}. Find the max executors and the bottleneck.
Variant 1
By RAM 80,000/8 = 10,000; by CPU 20,000/4 = 5,000; max 5,000, CPU is the bottleneck.
The admin changes Samza tasks to {4 GB, 1 vCPU}. Samza queue: 750 nodes = 48,000 GB, 12,000 vCPU (given). New max and bottleneck?
Variant 2
By RAM 48,000/4 = 12,000; by CPU 12,000/1 = 12,000; equal at 12,000, so RAM and CPU run out together (balanced).
Why must you take the minimum of the RAM limit and the CPU limit?
Why
A container needs both its RAM and its vCPUs on the same node. Whichever resource runs out first stops new containers, so the smaller count is the real ceiling and that resource is the bottleneck. YARN's DRF (Dominant Resource Fairness) exists for exactly this multi-resource case.
Card: Schedulers and capacity planning →

Parquet predicate pushdown: WHERE score > 90 on 10 TB reads 50 GBWeek 5 · W05 P1 s22-s23

very likely
GivenQuery WHERE score > 90. Footer stats: Row Group 1 score in [60, 85], Row Group 2 score in [85, 99]. Slide: a 10 TB Parquet query may physically read only 50 GB.
Worked solution · 5 steps (tap)
  1. Read the file footer only: min/max per column chunk per row group.
  2. Row Group 1: max 85 < 90, so no row can match. Skip the whole row group (no I/O).
  3. Row Group 2: range [85, 99] overlaps > 90, so it must be read.
  4. Inside Row Group 2 read only the score column chunk.
  5. Data read 50 GB of 10 TB = 0.5%, a reduction of 99.5%, about 200x less I/O.
AnswerSkip RG1, read only the score chunk of RG2; 10 TB to 50 GB is 200x less data (99.5% saved).
Practice · 3
Footer stats for amount: RG1 [0, 4,000], RG2 [3,500, 9,000], RG3 [12,000, 20,000]. Query WHERE amount > 10,000. Which row groups are read?
Variant 1
Only RG3 (min 12,000 > 10,000, all rows may match). RG1 max 4,000 and RG2 max 9,000 are below 10,000, so both are skipped.
A 4 TB Parquet table: after pushdown and column pruning Spark reads 80 GB. Earlier step given: speedup = data size / data read. Find the speedup.
Variant 2
4,000 GB / 80 GB = 50x less I/O.
Why can Parquet skip a row group without opening it, and why is no Spark setting needed?
Why
Each row group's footer stores min/max per column chunk; if the predicate cannot be true inside [min, max] the reader never touches those bytes. Spark enables Parquet filter pushdown by default (spark.sql.parquet.filterPushdown=true), so the saving is automatic.
Card: Row vs columnar storage and Parquet →

LinkedIn consolidation: 45% to 78% utilisation = 73% more workWeek 5 · W05 P2 s19, s21, s27

very likely
GivenThree siloed clusters ran at 45% average utilisation. One consolidated YARN cluster ran at 78%.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Work done is proportional to utilisation x capacity; capacity is unchanged.
  2. Ratio = 78 / 45 = 1.733.
  3. Extra workload = 1.733 - 1 = 73.3%, about 73%.
  4. Note: the gain is 33 percentage points, but 73% in relative workload.
Answer78/45 = 1.733: the same hardware served about 73% more workload.
Practice · 3
A bank merges two clusters running at 40% into one YARN cluster that runs at 70%. Given: extra work = U_new / U_old - 1. How much more work does the same hardware do?
Variant 1
70/40 - 1 = 75% more.
A cluster at 50% utilisation must take 60% more workload with no new nodes. What utilisation is needed?
Variant 2
50% x 1.6 = 80%.
Why did one shared cluster beat three separate clusters on utilisation?
Why
Each silo was idle at different times and could not lend its spare capacity. One YARN cluster pools all nodes, so idle capacity in one queue is borrowed by another (and reclaimed by pre-emption), and cross-cluster data copies disappear.
Card: Schedulers and capacity planning →

bKash archive: ORC + Zstd gives 60% size reduction vs CSVWeek 5 · W05 P1 s26

likely
GivenCold data older than 2 years moves to ORC + Zstd, about 60% smaller than CSV.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. New size = old size x (1 - 0.60) = 0.40 x CSV size.
  2. Example: 100 TB of CSV becomes 100 x 0.40 = 40 TB.
  3. Saving = 60 TB of storage (before HDFS 3x replication; with it, 180 TB of raw disk).
AnswerArchived size = 40% of the CSV size (100 TB to 40 TB).
Practice · 3
bKash has 250 TB of CSV older than 2 years. Given: ORC + Zstd is 60% smaller. What is the archived size?
Variant 1
250 x 0.40 = 100 TB.
The archive (ORC + Zstd) is 36 TB. How big was the CSV?
Variant 2
36 / 0.40 = 90 TB.
Why use Zstd for the archive but Snappy for the analytics layer?
Why
Snappy is fast with medium ratio: right for data queried every day. Zstd gives high compression at good speed, so it cuts long-term storage cost for cold data that is rarely read.
Card: File formats: Avro, Parquet, ORC →

YARN scale numbers: 6,000 vs 4,000 nodes; PYMK 18 h to 4 hWeek 5 · W05 P2 s10, s19

likely
GivenPaper: YARN tested on 6,000 nodes with 100,000 concurrent tasks vs Hadoop 1.x's 4,000-node limit; RM handled 1,000 heartbeats/s. LinkedIn: PYMK recompute 18 h on MR1, 4 h on YARN; 400,000 peak containers on 5,000 nodes.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Scale gain = (6,000 - 4,000) / 4,000 = 50% more nodes.
  2. PYMK speedup = 18 / 4 = 4.5x; time saved = 14/18 = 77.8%.
  3. Containers per node at peak = 400,000 / 5,000 = 80.
  4. Heartbeats: 6,000 NMs at 1,000/s means each NM can report about every 6 s.
Answer50% beyond the old ceiling; PYMK 4.5x faster; about 80 containers per node at peak.
Practice · 3
A job took 12 h on MR1 and 3 h on YARN with Spark. Given: speedup = T_old / T_new. Find the speedup and the time saved.
Variant 1
12/3 = 4x; saved 75%.
The RM processes 1,000 heartbeats per second. A cluster has 8,000 NodeManagers, each sending one heartbeat per interval. What is the shortest interval the RM can sustain?
Variant 2
8,000 / 1,000 = 8 s per heartbeat per node.
Why was Hadoop 1.x stuck near 4,000 nodes?
Why
A single JobTracker did both cluster resource management and per-job scheduling and monitoring for every task, so it became the bottleneck. YARN moved per-job work into one ApplicationMaster per job, leaving the RM only global scheduling.
Card: YARN and its three components →

Capacity Scheduler queue shares (a2i 60/30/10, LinkedIn 40/25/15/10/7/3)Week 5 · W05 P1 s13-s14; W05 P2 s17-s18

likely
Givena2i cluster: Queue A 60% (DGHS batch), Queue B 30% (Spark streaming), Queue C 10% (ad-hoc Hive). LinkedIn 5,000 nodes: production 40%, spark 25%, samza 15%, adhoc 10%, tez 7%, reserve 3%.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Guaranteed nodes = cluster nodes x queue share.
  2. LinkedIn: production 2,000, spark 1,250, samza 750, adhoc 500, tez 350, reserve 150 nodes.
  3. Check: shares sum to 100%.
  4. Idle capacity in one queue can be borrowed by others and is reclaimed by pre-emption (LinkedIn: 30-second warning).
AnswerProduction 2,000, spark 1,250, samza 750, adhoc 500, tez 350, reserve 150 nodes; queue B on a2i can never take queue A's guaranteed 60%.
Practice · 3
a2i runs on a 400-node cluster with A 60%, B 30%, C 10%. Given: guaranteed = nodes x share. How many nodes is Queue B guaranteed?
Variant 1
400 x 0.30 = 120 nodes.
Engineering 60%, Finance 40% on 1,000 nodes. Finance is idle and Engineering borrows its share. How many nodes can Engineering use now, and what happens when Finance submits a job?
Variant 2
Engineering can elastically use all 1,000 nodes; when Finance submits, pre-emption reclaims its guaranteed 400 nodes.
Why does a shared cluster use the Capacity Scheduler instead of FIFO?
Why
FIFO runs jobs in order, so one long job starves everyone else. Capacity gives each team a guaranteed share (an SLA), so ad-hoc analyst queries cannot starve revenue pipelines, while still lending idle capacity to busy queues.
Card: Schedulers and capacity planning →

Analytical A1: wall-clock time for 100 K-means iterations (500 vs 5,000 MB/s)Week 6 · W06 P1 s38 (Analytical A1)

very likely
Given50 GB bKash data, 100 iterations. HDFS read speed 500 MB/s, RAM cache read 5,000 MB/s. Assume HDFS write runs at the same 500 MB/s (not stated on the slide).
Worked solution · 5 steps (tap)
  1. One HDFS pass: 50,000 MB / 500 MB/s = 100 s.
  2. MapReduce per iteration = read + write = 200 s; total = 100 x 200 = 20,000 s = 5.56 h. Total HDFS I/O 10 TB.
  3. Spark: first read from HDFS 100 s; 99 more passes from RAM at 50,000/5,000 = 10 s each = 990 s.
  4. Spark total = 100 + 990 = 1,090 s, about 18.2 min. HDFS I/O 50 GB.
  5. Speedup = 20,000 / 1,090 = 18.3x.
AnswerMapReduce about 20,000 s (5.56 h); Spark about 1,090 s (18.2 min); about 18.3x faster. Spark loses its edge if the data does not fit in RAM, or the job is a single pass.
Practice · 3
Given: one HDFS pass over 50 GB takes 100 s and one RAM pass takes 10 s. Spark reads HDFS once, then RAM for the remaining iterations. Total Spark time for 10 iterations?
Variant 1
100 + 9 x 10 = 190 s.
Given: MapReduce takes 200 s per iteration (read + write). How long do 10 iterations take, and what is the speedup over the 190 s Spark run?
Variant 2
10 x 200 = 2000 s; 2,000/190 = 10.5x.
Under what conditions would Spark not outperform MapReduce?
Why
When the working set does not fit in cluster RAM (Spark spills to disk), when the job is a single pass over the data (nothing to reuse; slides say gains shrink to 2-5x), or when each executor's memory overhead (about 8 GB minimum) is too costly on a very large cluster.
Card: Why Spark: the MapReduce iteration bottleneck →

Analytical A2: executor with partitions 3 and 7 crashes (10 partitions)Week 6 · W06 P1 s14-s15, s21, s38 (Analytical A2)

very likely
Giveninput -> filteredRDD -> mappedRDD -> reducedRDD, 10 partitions each. The executor holding partitions 3 and 7 of reducedRDD crashes.
Worked solution · 5 steps (tap)
  1. Driver: the executor stops heartbeating and its tasks fail; the driver marks partitions 3 and 7 (and anything else cached there) lost.
  2. Lineage lookup: reducedRDD <- mappedRDD <- filteredRDD <- input (HDFS).
  3. If all steps are narrow: recompute only partitions 3 and 7 of filteredRDD and mappedRDD from HDFS blocks 3 and 7: 2 input partitions, 2 x 3 = 6 partition computations.
  4. If reducedRDD comes from groupByKey (wide): partition 3 of reducedRDD needs data from all 10 mappedRDD partitions.
  5. Worst case (shuffle files lost with the executor and nothing cached): recompute all 10 partitions of filteredRDD and mappedRDD, re-shuffle, then rebuild partitions 3 and 7: 10 + 10 + 2 = 22 partition computations, plus re-reading all 10 HDFS blocks.
AnswerNarrow: 2 partitions per RDD (from 2 HDFS blocks). Wide (groupByKey) worst case: all 10 parent partitions recomputed and re-shuffled, 5x the input re-read.
Practice · 3
A job with 20 partitions, all narrow (map, filter). An executor holding 4 partitions dies. Given: narrow recovery recomputes only the lost partitions from their single parents. How many input partitions are re-read?
Variant 1
4 (one parent per lost partition).
Same job but the last step is reduceByKey over 20 partitions and no shuffle output survives. How many parent partitions must be recomputed in the worst case?
Variant 2
All 20, because every reduce partition depends on every map partition.
Why do long or wide lineages get checkpointed to HDFS?
Why
Recomputing a lost partition through a wide dependency drags in every parent partition, and a long chain multiplies that. A checkpoint cuts the lineage so recovery starts from the saved copy instead of from the original input.
Card: RDDs and lineage-based fault tolerance →

Daytona GraySort 2013: 100 TB in 23 min on 206 nodes vs Hadoop 72 min on 2,100Week 6 · W06 P2 s2, s13-s14, s20; W06 P1 s9

very likely
GivenHadoop record (Yahoo! 2012): 100 TB in 72 min on 2,100 nodes. Spark (Databricks 2013): 100 TB in 23 min on 206 EC2 i2.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 244 GB RAM, 8 x 800 GB SSD each). Input stored with 3x replication.
Worked solution · 6 steps (tap)
  1. Faster: 72 / 23 = 3.13x (slide: 3.1x).
  2. Fewer nodes: 2,100 / 206 = 10.19x (slide: 10.2x).
  3. Efficiency per node = (72 x 2,100) / (23 x 206) = 151,200 / 4,738 = 31.9x (slide: 32x).
  4. Total RAM = 206 x 244 GB = 50,264 GB = 50.3 TB; SSD per node 8 x 800 GB = 6.4 TB, total 206 x 6.4 = 1,318 TB = 1.32 PB.
  5. On disk with 3x replication: 100 x 3 = 300 TB.
  6. Throughput = 100 TB / 23 min = 4.35 TB/min (the slide prints 4.27, which would need 23.4 min).
Answer3.1x faster on 10.2x fewer nodes, about 31.91x more work per node; 4.35 TB/min by recomputation.
Practice · 3
Yahoo! 2009 sorted 100 TB on 3,800 nodes in 173 min. Spark: 206 nodes, 23 min. Given: efficiency per node = (T_old x N_old) / (T_new x N_new). Compute it.
Variant 1
(173 x 3,800) / (23 x 206) = 657,400 / 4,738 = 138.8x.
A cluster of 100 nodes, each 256 GB RAM and 8 x 1 TB SSD. Total RAM and total SSD?
Variant 2
RAM 100 x 256 = 25,600 GB = 25.6 TB; SSD 100 x 8 = 800 TB.
Why does node-time (time x nodes) matter more than raw speed in this comparison?
Why
Spark finished 3.1x faster while using 10.2x fewer machines, so it did the same job with about 1/32 of the machine-minutes. That shows the gain is from the design (sort-based shuffle on SSDs, off-heap sort buffers, fewer stages), not from throwing more hardware at it.
Card: Why Spark: the MapReduce iteration bottleneck →

K-means, 100 iterations on 50 GB: MapReduce 10 TB disk I/O vs Spark 50 GBWeek 6 · W06 P1 s6-s7

very likely
Given50 GB on HDFS, 100 iterations. MapReduce reads and writes 50 GB per iteration. Spark reads once and caches in RAM.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. MapReduce: 100 x (50 GB read + 50 GB write) = 10,000 GB = 10 TB.
  2. Spark: iteration 1 reads 50 GB from HDFS; iterations 2-100 read RAM. HDFS I/O = 50 GB.
  3. Ratio = 10,000 / 50 = 200x less disk I/O.
Answer10 TB vs 50 GB: about 200x less disk I/O for Spark.
Practice · 3
A bKash model trains for 20 iterations over 200 GB. Given: MapReduce disk I/O = k x (read + write). Find MapReduce's total disk I/O.
Variant 1
20 x (200 + 200) = 8,000 GB = 8 TB.
Same job: MapReduce does 8 TB of disk I/O; Spark reads 200 GB once. How many times less disk I/O does Spark do?
Variant 2
8,000 / 200 = 40x.
Why does MapReduce pay disk I/O on every iteration?
Why
Each iteration is a separate MapReduce job, and MapReduce writes every job's output to HDFS before the next job can start. It has no way to keep the working set in memory across jobs, so an iterative algorithm reads and writes the full dataset every pass.
Card: Why Spark: the MapReduce iteration bottleneck →

RDD paper benchmarks: logistic regression 132x, k-means 30xWeek 6 · W06 P2 s10

very likely
GivenLogistic regression, 10 iterations: Hadoop 127 s/iteration, Spark (MEMORY_ONLY) 0.96 s/iteration. K-means, 10 iterations: Hadoop 150 s vs Spark 5 s.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. LR speedup = 127 / 0.96 = 132.3x, about 132x.
  2. LR total over 10 iterations: Hadoop 1,270 s vs Spark 9.6 s.
  3. K-means speedup = 150 / 5 = 30x.
AnswerAbout 132.29x for logistic regression (1,270 s vs 9.6 s over 10 iterations) and 30x for k-means.
Practice · 3
A Spark LR job takes 1.2 s per iteration; Hadoop takes 120 s. Given: speedup = T_old / T_new. Find the speedup.
Variant 1
120 / 1.2 = 100x.
Hadoop 127 s per iteration, Spark 0.96 s per iteration. How long do 50 iterations take on each?
Variant 2
Hadoop 50 x 127 = 6,350 s; Spark 50 x 0.96 = 48 s.
Why is the logistic regression gain (132x) bigger than the k-means gain (30x)?
Why
Logistic regression does very little CPU work per pass, so its time is almost all I/O, which caching removes. K-means does more computation per point per iteration, so a larger share of its time is CPU that caching cannot remove. (Reasoning, not stated on the slide.)

Why MapReduce sorts slowly: each byte written twice (~200 TB extra at 100 TB)Week 6 · W06 P2 s13, s15

likely
GivenMapReduce's sort phase writes intermediate data to disk twice per byte (spill + merge). Spark's sort-based shuffle writes sorted runs once, eliminating about 120 TB of extra I/O at 100 TB.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. MapReduce extra disk I/O = 2 writes x 100 TB = 200 TB.
  2. Spark removes about 120 TB of that, leaving about 80 TB of shuffle I/O.
  3. Reduction in extra I/O = 120 / 200 = 60%.
AnswerAbout 200 TB of extra disk I/O for MapReduce; Spark's sort shuffle saves about 120 TB (60%).
Practice · 3
A 40 TB sort on MapReduce writes every intermediate byte twice. Given: extra I/O = 2 x data. How much extra disk I/O?
Variant 1
2 x 40 = 80 TB.
Spark's shuffle cuts that extra I/O by 60%. How much remains for the 40 TB sort?
Variant 2
80 x 0.40 = 32 TB.
Why is the shuffle the bottleneck both at GraySort and in production Spark?
Why
A shuffle is a wide dependency: every output partition needs data from every input partition, so data crosses the network and hits disk, and it forms a stage barrier. Minimising wide dependencies is the main Spark tuning skill.
Card: Narrow vs wide dependencies, stages and shuffle →

Hash partitioner: key.hashCode() % numPartitionsWeek 6 · W06 P2 s10; W06 P1 s21-s22

likely
GivenSpark's default partitioner sends a key to partition key.hashCode() % numPartitions. For an integer key, hashCode() is the value itself (Java behaviour, general knowledge).
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Take the key's hash.
  2. Divide by the number of partitions and keep the remainder.
  3. Example: key 17, 4 partitions: 17 % 4 = 1, so partition 1.
  4. All pairs with the same key land in the same partition, which is what reduceByKey and join need.
Answerpartition = hash(key) mod numPartitions; key 17 with 4 partitions goes to partition 1.
Practice · 3
An RDD of (customer_id, amount) has 8 partitions. Given: partition = key % 8. Where does customer_id 1,234 go?
Variant 1
1,234 % 8 = 2, partition 2.
Keys 10, 20, 30, 40 with 5 partitions. Which partitions are used, and what is the problem?
Variant 2
[0, 0, 0, 0]: all land in partition 0, a hot spot (skew). Range or custom partitioning would spread them.
Why do two RDDs partitioned with the same partitioner join without a shuffle?
Why
Matching keys already sit in the same-numbered partition of both RDDs, so partition i joins only with partition i (a narrow dependency). Without co-partitioning, rows must be reshuffled across the network first.
Card: Narrow vs wide dependencies, stages and shuffle →

HotCloud claim: 10 iterations over 100 GB at 100 MB/s costs about 3 hours of I/OWeek 6 · W06 P2 s4

likely
GivenFor k iterations MapReduce pays k x HDFS read + k x HDFS write. Spinning disk 100 MB/s, 10 iterations, 100 GB.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. Reads only: 10 x 100 GB = 1,000 GB = 1,000,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 10,000 s = 2.78 h, about 3 h.
  2. Reads + writes (the slide's own formula): 2,000 GB / 100 MB/s = 20,000 s = 5.56 h.
  3. So the slide's 3 hours matches the read side only; with writes included it is about 5.6 h. Either way it is hours of pure I/O, which Spark avoids by caching after the first read.
AnswerAbout 2.8 h counting reads only (the slide's 3 h); 5.6 h if writes are counted too.
Practice · 3
A graph job runs 20 iterations over 50 GB on disk at 100 MB/s. Given: read time per iteration = 50,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 500 s. Total read time?
Variant 1
20 x 500 = 10,000 s = 2.78 h.
Same job, Spark: first read from disk takes 500 s, later passes come from RAM at 2,000 MB/s. Time for one RAM pass?
Variant 2
50,000 / 2,000 = 25 s.
What is a working set, and why can't MapReduce exploit it?
Why
A working set is data reused across many parallel operations (the same training set every gradient step, the same table in repeated queries, the same graph in every BFS pass). MapReduce has no cache between jobs, so it rereads it from HDFS every time; Spark keeps it as a cached RDD.
Card: Why Spark: the MapReduce iteration bottleneck →

Live Exercise: RDD lineage, lazy evaluation and cache speedupWeek 6 · W06 P2 s18 (Live Exercise)

likely
GivenWord count on README.md with sc local[4]: flatMap -> map -> reduceByKey. Time counts.count() before and after cache(); compare reduceByKey with groupByKey in the Spark UI. Sample timings (not on the slide): first count 2.40 s, cached count 0.012 s.
Worked solution · 5 steps (tap)
  1. Before any action, toDebugString shows the lineage only: no job has run (lazy evaluation).
  2. First count() triggers the whole DAG: read, flatMap, map, shuffle for reduceByKey.
  3. counts.cache() marks the RDD for caching; the warm-up count() fills the cache; toDebugString now shows the RDD as cached in memory.
  4. Speedup = 2.40 / 0.012 = 200x.
  5. groupByKey ships every (word, 1) pair across the shuffle; reduceByKey combines locally first, so shuffle read/write bytes are much smaller.
AnswerCached count is served from memory; with the sample timings the speedup is 200x. reduceByKey shuffles fewer bytes than groupByKey.
Practice · 3
A student times count(): 3.6 s uncached, 0.045 s cached. Given: speedup = uncached / cached. Report the speedup.
Variant 1
3.6 / 0.045 = 80x.
One partition holds 1,000 (word, 1) pairs covering 50 distinct words. How many records leave that partition in the shuffle with groupByKey vs reduceByKey?
Variant 2
groupByKey: 1,000; reduceByKey: 50 (one partial sum per word).
Why is the first count() slow even though the script defined everything earlier?
Why
Transformations are lazy: they only record the lineage. Nothing is read or computed until an action, so the first count() pays for the full DAG. Only after cache() plus one action does a later count() read from memory.
Card: Transformations, actions and lazy evaluation →

Speedup ranges: 10-100x iterative, 2-5x single pass, DataFrame 10-100x over RDDWeek 6 · W06 P1 s26, s31-s32; W06 P2 s16

likely
GivenSpark is 10-100x faster on iterative workloads; for single-pass ETL larger than RAM, 2-5x. DataFrames are 10-100x faster than RDDs for structured data. Spark executors need about 8 GB minimum. Use Spark for >2 iterations over the same data.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. A 10-hour iterative MapReduce job at 10-100x becomes 6 min to 60 min.
  2. A 10-hour single-pass ETL at 2-5x becomes 2 h to 5 h.
  3. Executor memory floor: 50 executors x 8 GB = 400 GB of RAM before any data is cached.
AnswerIterative: 10 h becomes 6-60 min; single pass: 2-5 h; 50 executors need at least 400 GB RAM.
Practice · 3
A nightly single-pass ETL takes 6 h on MapReduce. Given: single-pass gains are 2-5x. What range of Spark run times should you expect?
Variant 1
6/5 = 1.2 h to 6/2 = 3 h.
A cluster runs 200 Spark executors at the 8 GB minimum. How much RAM is reserved just for executor overhead?
Variant 2
200 x 8 = 1,600 GB = 1.6 TB.
Why is in-memory processing 'a multiplier, not a panacea'?
Why
The gain comes from reusing data held in RAM. A single pass reads each byte once, so there is nothing to reuse and the speedup shrinks to 2-5x; and data larger than RAM spills to disk. Spark's JVM memory overhead can even hurt with many small files or high-cardinality groupBy.
Card: DataFrames, Spark SQL and the ecosystem →

Analytical A1: partition and bucket a 5 TB e-commerce tableWeek 7 · W07 P1 s32 (Analytical A1)

very likely
Given5 TB table (txn_id, user_id, product_id, amount, country, txn_date). Reports filter by country and txn_date; joins with a 10 M-row user profile table on user_id. Assume 1 year of data and 10 countries (assumption, not on slide).
Worked solution · 5 steps (tap)
  1. Partition on txn_date and country (both low-cardinality and in every WHERE). Never on user_id.
  2. Partitions = 365 x 10 = 3,650; average partition = 5,000,000 MB / 3,650 = 1,370 MB.
  3. Bucket on user_id, the join key, with the same bucket count in the user table.
  4. Pick N so files are near the 128 MB HDFS block: 1,370 / 128 = 10.7, so 8 or 16 buckets; N = 16 gives 85.62 MB files (58,400 files).
  5. DDL: CREATE TABLE txns (txn_id BIGINT, user_id BIGINT, product_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE) PARTITIONED BY (country STRING, txn_date DATE) CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 16 BUCKETS STORED AS ORC;
AnswerPARTITIONED BY (country, txn_date), CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 16 BUCKETS, ORC; about 85.62 MB per bucket file.
Practice · 3
A 2 TB table has 1,000 partitions. Given: partition size = 2,000,000 MB / 1,000 = 2,000 MB. How many buckets give files of about 128 MB?
Variant 1
2,000 / 128 = 15.6, so 16 buckets (125 MB files).
The user table is bucketed into 32 buckets on user_id, the transaction table into 16. Can Hive do a bucket map join?
Variant 2
Not as the slide defines it: a bucket map join needs both tables bucketed on the join key with the same number of buckets, so use the same N (16 or 32) on both. (General knowledge: Hive also accepts one count being a multiple of the other, and 32 is a multiple of 16.)
Why choose the bucket count from file size rather than picking a large number?
Why
Too many buckets make many small files, which waste NameNode memory and launch too many tasks; too few make huge files with little parallelism. Aim near the 128 MB block size per bucket file.
Card: Bucketing and bucket map join →

Discussion Q2: ALS model size, 75 M users x 30 M songs at rank 50Week 7 · W07 P2 s18 (Discussion Q2); W05 P2 s23

very likely
GivenALS factorises a 75 M-user x 30 M-song matrix at rank k = 50, 4 bytes per float. Compare with the 5,000-node YARN cluster (64 GB per node, W05 Live Exercise).
Worked solution · 5 steps (tap)
  1. ALS stores one k-vector per user and per song: (users + songs) x k floats.
  2. (75,000,000 + 30,000,000) x 50 = 5,250,000,000 floats.
  3. x 4 bytes = 21,000,000,000 bytes = 21 GB.
  4. Cluster RAM = 5,000 x 64 GB = 320,000 GB = 320 TB.
  5. Model is 21 / 320,000 = 0.0066% of cluster RAM: it fits easily.
Answer21 GB; fits in the 320 TB of aggregate RAM many times over.
Practice · 3
Rank is raised to k = 100, everything else the same. Given: size = (users + songs) x k x 4 B. New model size?
Variant 1
105,000,000 x 100 x 4 = 42 GB.
Why is the full 75 M x 30 M matrix never stored? Compute its size at 4 bytes per cell.
Variant 2
75e6 x 30e6 x 4 = 9.0e+15 bytes = 9 PB; ALS stores only the factors.
Why is ALS run in Spark rather than as HiveQL?
Why
ALS is iterative: it alternates solving user and song factors many times over the same data. Spark caches the data and factors in memory across iterations; HiveQL on MapReduce would write to HDFS every pass. Spotify used HiveQL for the co-occurrence aggregation (one SQL pass) and Spark for ALS.
Card: Case study: Spotify Discover Weekly →

Bucketing: hash(user_id) % N; bucket map join on 4 or 32 bucketsWeek 7 · W07 P1 s23-s24

very likely
GivenCLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO N BUCKETS. Rows where hash(column) % N = k go to bucket file k. Slide examples: 4 buckets in the diagram, 32 in the DDL. For an integer key, hash = the value (general knowledge).
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. user_id 98 with 4 buckets: 98 % 4 = 2, bucket 2.
  2. Both tables bucketed on user_id with the same N: rows with equal user_id sit in the same bucket number in both.
  3. Bucket map join pairs bucket i of sales with bucket i of users only: with 32 buckets, 32 small joins instead of one full shuffle join.
  4. Each partition (e.g. year=2024/month=01) holds N bucket files.
AnswerBucket = hash % N (98 % 4 = 2); a bucket map join does N matched bucket-pair joins with no full shuffle.
Practice · 3
A users table is CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS. Given: bucket = user_id % 32. Which bucket holds user_id 1,000?
Variant 1
1,000 % 32 = 8, bucket 8.
A table partitioned by 365 dt values is bucketed into 32 buckets. How many bucket files exist, and what is their average size if the table is 1.168 TB?
Variant 2
365 x 32 = 11,680 files; 1,168,000 MB / 11,680 = 100 MB each.
Partitioning and bucketing both split data. Why is bucketing the one that speeds up joins?
Why
Partitioning skips directories by filter value but leaves rows with the same join key scattered. Bucketing places equal keys in the same-numbered file in both tables, so Hive joins bucket i with bucket i and skips the sort-merge shuffle. Both tables need the same bucket count on the join key.
Card: Bucketing and bucket map join →

Discussion Q1: output size of GROUP BY song_a, song_b over 30 M songsWeek 7 · W07 P2 s16-s18 (Discussion Q1); W07 P2 s20 (Live Exercise)

very likely
GivenCo-occurrence query GROUP BY song_a, song_b over 2 billion playlist rows, 30 M songs, pairs counted once (song_a < song_b), HAVING COUNT(*) > 5.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Upper bound on distinct pairs = 30 M x (30 M - 1) / 2 = 4.500e+14 (about 4.5 x 10^14).
  2. Real output is far smaller: only pairs that actually co-occur, and HAVING > 5 drops rare ones; it is bounded by the pairs generated from playlists.
  3. A playlist of L songs gives L(L-1)/2 pairs: 20 songs give 190 pairs.
  4. To shrink the shuffle: bucket playlist_songs by playlist_id (so the self-join is bucket-local) and partition by week/dt so only recent data is read.
AnswerAt most about 4.50e+14 pairs; actual output limited to co-occurring pairs above the HAVING threshold. Bucket on playlist_id, partition on date.
Practice · 3
A playlist has 30 songs. Given: pairs per playlist = L(L-1)/2. How many song pairs does it emit?
Variant 1
30 x 29 / 2 = 435.
Live Exercise data: 10,000 rows spread over 1,000 playlists, so about 10 songs per playlist. Estimate the pair rows produced by the self-join (a.song_id < b.song_id).
Variant 2
1,000 x 10 x 9 / 2 = 45,000 pair rows.
Why does the query use a.song_id < b.song_id in the self-join?
Why
Without it every pair appears twice (A,B and B,A) plus self-pairs (A,A). The < condition keeps each unordered pair once, halving the shuffle and output.
Card: Case study: Spotify Discover Weekly →

Map-side aggregation: 50 M rows, 200 countries, shuffle cut by ~250,000xWeek 7 · W07 P2 s10

very likely
GivenSELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY country on 50 million rows with 200 countries. Hive does partial aggregation in the mapper (combiner pattern) before shuffling.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Without map-side aggregation every row is shuffled as (country, 1): 50,000,000 records.
  2. With it, the output is at most one (country, partial count) per country: 200 records (if one mapper; M mappers send up to M x 200).
  3. Reduction = 50,000,000 / 200 = 250,000x.
  4. With 10 mappers: 10 x 200 = 2,000 records, still 25,000x less.
Answer50,000,000 records become 200: about 250,000x less shuffle data.
Practice · 3
A Hive table of 80 million click rows is grouped by 400 browser versions. Given: with map-side aggregation, one record per group leaves the map side. What is the shuffle reduction?
Variant 1
80,000,000 / 400 = 200,000x.
Same 80 M rows, 400 groups, but run by 20 mappers, each emitting one partial count per group. How many records are shuffled?
Variant 2
20 x 400 = 8,000 records (10,000x less than 80 M).
Why is map-side aggregation safe for COUNT but not for every function?
Why
COUNT and SUM can be split into partial results and added up later (they are associative), so combining in the mapper gives the same final answer. A function like median cannot be built from partial medians, so it cannot be pre-aggregated that way.
Card: Hive architecture and query compilation →

year=2024/month=01 reads 1 sub-directory, not 36 months; 100 M user_id partitionsWeek 7 · W07 P1 s19-s21

very likely
GivenTable partitioned by (year, month) over 3 years: 36 sub-directories. Query WHERE year=2024 AND month=01. Warning: partitioning a 100 M user table on user_id would create 100 M directories.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Partitions = 3 years x 12 months = 36.
  2. The query reads 1 of 36 = 2.78%; 35 directories skipped.
  3. If data is even and the job is I/O bound, job time drops by about 36x.
  4. On user_id: one directory per distinct value = 100,000,000 directories, each a NameNode metadata object, which overflows NameNode memory.
Answer1 of 36 directories (2.8%); partitioning on user_id would mean 100 M directories.
Practice · 3
Daily partitions (dt) over 2 years. Given: partitions = 2 x 365. A dashboard query reads the last 7 days. What fraction is read?
Variant 1
7 / 730 = 0.96%.
An engineer partitions a 20 M-row orders table by order_id. How many partition directories result, and is this a good idea?
Variant 2
20,000,000 directories (one per order). No: high cardinality causes partition explosion and NameNode metadata overflow; partition by date instead and bucket by order_id.
Why should partition keys be low-cardinality columns used often in WHERE?
Why
Each distinct value is a directory. Low cardinality (date, country, status) keeps the directory count small, and frequent filtering on it means most queries skip most data. High cardinality creates millions of tiny directories and files that overload the NameNode.
Card: Partitioning and partition pruning →

Partition pruning: 3 of 365 x 200 = 73,000 partitions readWeek 7 · W07 P2 s11

very likely
Givenplay_events partitioned by (dt, country): 365 days x 200 countries. Query WHERE p.dt = '2024-10-01' AND p.country IN ('BD','IN','US').
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Total partitions = 365 x 200 = 73,000.
  2. The filter fixes one dt and three countries: 1 x 3 = 3 partitions.
  3. Fraction read = 3 / 73,000 = 0.0041%; 72,997 partitions skipped.
  4. The Metastore holds each partition's HDFS path, so Hive picks the 3 directories without listing all files.
AnswerHive reads 3 of 73,000 partitions (0.0041%).
Practice · 3
A sales table is partitioned by (year, month) over 3 years. Given: total partitions = years x 12. A query asks for year=2024 AND month IN (1, 2). How many partitions are read out of the total?
Variant 1
2 of 3 x 12 = 36; fraction 5.6%.
A 7.3 TB table is spread evenly over 73,000 partitions. A query hits 3. How much data is read?
Variant 2
7.3 TB / 73,000 = 100 MB per partition; 3 x 100 = 300 MB.
Why must the WHERE clause filter on the partition column itself for pruning to work?
Why
Pruning works at planning time from the Metastore's list of partition directories. Hive can only skip a directory if the predicate is on the column that names it (dt, country). A filter on another column must be checked row by row, so every directory is read.
Card: Partitioning and partition pruning →

Spotify: partitioning play_events by week cut co-occurrence HiveQL from 8 h to 2 hWeek 7 · W07 P2 s18

very likely
GivenPartitioning play_events by week reduced the co-occurrence HiveQL from 8 hours to 2 hours. Daily retraining would cost 7x the compute of weekly.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. Speedup = 8 / 2 = 4x.
  2. Time saved = (8 - 2) / 8 = 75%.
  3. Retraining: weekly costs 1 unit per week; daily costs 7 units per week (7x).
Answer4x faster, 75% of the time saved; daily retraining would cost 7x the weekly compute.
Practice · 3
A HiveQL report drops from 6 h to 45 min after partitioning by date. Given: speedup = T_old / T_new. Find the speedup.
Variant 1
360 / 45 = 8x.
Weekly retraining costs 140 CPU-hours. What would daily retraining cost per week?
Variant 2
7 x 140 = 980 CPU-hours.
Why did the choice of partition column change latency by hours?
Why
The co-occurrence job only needs recent weeks. With play_events partitioned by week, Hive reads just those week directories and skips the rest; partitioned on a column the query does not filter on, it scans everything.

Analytical A2: top 5 products by revenue in 2023, compiled to MapReduceWeek 7 · W07 P1 s32 (Analytical A2); W07 P2 s11

likely
GivenSELECT product_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM transactions WHERE YEAR(txn_date) = 2023 GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 5. Sample: 3 mappers, each sees all 1,000 products.
Worked solution · 5 steps (tap)
  1. Job 1 Map: read rows, apply the 2023 filter, emit (product_id, amount); map-side aggregation emits (product_id, partial sum).
  2. Shuffle key: product_id.
  3. Job 1 Reduce: SUM per product -> (product_id, revenue).
  4. Job 2: global sort by revenue DESC and LIMIT 5 (one reducer sees all totals). With 3 mappers x 1,000 products the shuffle carries at most 3,000 partial sums.
  5. On Tez: the two jobs become one DAG; no HDFS write between the aggregate and the sort.
AnswerMap emits (product_id, amount); shuffle on product_id; reduce sums; a second stage sorts and takes 5. Tez fuses the stages into one DAG with no intermediate HDFS write.
Practice · 3
Mappers emit partial sums per product. 5 mappers, 2,000 products, each mapper sees every product. Given: records shuffled = mappers x groups. How many records are shuffled?
Variant 1
5 x 2,000 = 10,000.
Without map-side aggregation, how many records would 30 million 2023 rows shuffle, and what is the saving vs 10,000?
Variant 2
30,000,000 records; 30,000,000 / 10,000 = 3,000x more.
Why does Tez make this query faster than MapReduce without changing the HiveQL?
Why
MapReduce runs the aggregate and the global sort as two separate jobs and writes Job 1's output to HDFS between them. Tez runs one DAG of tasks and passes data directly between stages, so the intermediate HDFS write and the second job start-up disappear.
Card: Hive architecture and query compilation →

Facebook Hive scale (2 PB, 15 TB/day, 7,500 queries) and Spotify event ratesWeek 7 · W07 P2 s4, s9-s10, s14; W07 P1 s11

likely
GivenFacebook 2010: 2 PB stored, 15 TB/day growth, 7,500+ queries/day, <15% failure rate, 200+ analysts. Spotify: about 3 billion events/day; its Hive Metastore catalogs over 1 million tables on a cluster processing 600 billion events/day.
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Yearly growth = 15 TB x 365 = 5,475 TB = 5.47 PB.
  2. Failures at most 15% of 7,500 = 1,125 queries/day.
  3. Queries per analyst = 7,500 / 200 = 37.5 per day.
  4. Spotify 3 B events/day / 86,400 s = 34,722 events/s.
AnswerAbout 5.47 PB/year growth; up to 1,125 failed queries/day; about 34,722 Spotify events per second.
Practice · 3
A data lake grows 15 TB per day. Given: yearly growth = daily x 365. How much after 2 years if it started at 2 PB?
Variant 1
2 PB + 2 x 5.475 PB = 12.95 PB.
600 billion events per day. Given: per second = daily / 86,400. Compute.
Variant 2
600e9 / 86,400 = 6,944,444 events/s.
Why do the slides call the Metastore 'as important as HDFS itself'?
Why
Hive cannot answer a single query without the Metastore: it holds table schemas, partition paths, SerDes and statistics. If it is corrupted, every table is unqueryable even though the data on HDFS is intact, so it runs as a replicated HA service.
Card: Hive architecture and query compilation →

Presto vs Hive+MR: 5-15 min vs 5-60 s; vectorised 1,024-row batchesWeek 7 · W07 P1 s17, s26

likely
GivenHive+MR: 5-15 min; Presto: 5-60 s. A COUNT(*) on 1 TB takes 5-10 min on MapReduce. Presto processes column chunks in batches of 1,024 rows. Presto is about 10x faster than Hive+MapReduce.
Worked solution · 3 steps (tap)
  1. Hive best and worst: 5 min = 300 s, 15 min = 900 s.
  2. Ratios: 300/60 = 5x (worst Presto vs best Hive) up to 900/5 = 180x; about 10x typical.
  3. Vectorised batches: 10,000,000 rows / 1,024 = 9,766, so 9,766 batches instead of 10 million row-at-a-time calls.
AnswerPresto is roughly 5x to 180x faster across the ranges (about 10x typical); 10 M rows run as 9,766 batches.
Practice · 3
A Hive+MR query takes 12 min. Given: Presto is about 10x faster for interactive queries. Estimate Presto's time.
Variant 1
12 x 60 / 10 = 72 s.
Presto reads a 2,048,000-row column chunk in 1,024-row batches. How many batches?
Variant 2
2,048,000 / 1,024 = 2,000.
Why is Presto faster than Hive+MapReduce for interactive queries?
Why
Presto pipelines data through the stages entirely in memory and never writes intermediate results to HDFS, while Hive+MR materialises data to HDFS between every MapReduce stage. Vectorised execution and a cost-based optimiser add more.

Analytical A1: bank pipeline, 10 M records nightly, 200 ms fraud, 5-minute dashboardWeek 8 · W08 P1 s9, s36 (Analytical A1)

very likely
Given(a) Sync 10 million customer records nightly from Oracle to Hadoop. (b) Fraud decision within 200 ms. (c) Risk dashboard no older than 5 minutes. Assume Sqoop runs 4 map tasks and a 2-hour batch window (assumptions).
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. (a) Sqoop import (JDBC, parallel map tasks split by primary-key range, incremental by last-value): 10,000,000 / 4 = 2,500,000 rows per mapper; over 2 h that is 1,389 rows/s overall.
  2. (b) Card swipes -> Kafka -> Spark Streaming (or Flink) scoring: only a stream path can answer in 200 ms.
  3. (c) Stream aggregates refreshed every <= 5 min: 288 refreshes per day.
  4. Architecture: Lambda fits (nightly Sqoop batch for accurate history and regulatory reports + Kafka speed layer); Kappa only if all history can be replayed from Kafka fast enough.
AnswerSqoop for (a), Kafka + Spark Streaming for (b) and (c); Lambda architecture.
Practice · 3
Sqoop imports 10 M rows with 8 map tasks. Given: rows per mapper = rows / mappers. How many rows does each read?
Variant 1
10,000,000 / 8 = 1,250,000.
A dashboard must be at most 5 minutes old. How many updates per day at least?
Variant 2
86,400 / 300 = 288.
Why not use Sqoop for the 200 ms fraud check?
Why
Sqoop is a batch tool that launches MapReduce jobs, usually nightly; its latency is hours. Fraud scoring needs each event processed as it arrives, which is what Kafka plus a stream processor gives.
Card: Batch ingestion: Sqoop and Flume →

Analytical A2: is the stream engine fast enough for Kappa replay?Week 8 · W08 P1 s25-s27, s36 (Analytical A2)

very likely
GivenKappa reprocesses by starting a new job at offset 0 and letting it catch up. Example: 7 days retained at Netflix's average rate (100 B events/day); the stream engine can process 10 M events/s (assumption).
Worked solution · 4 steps (tap)
  1. Events to replay = 7 x 100 B = 700 billion.
  2. Replay time = 700e9 / 10e6 = 70,000 s = 19.4 h.
  3. Live data keeps arriving at 1,157,407/s, so the new job gains 8,842,593/s on the head; catch-up time = 700e9 / 8,842,593 = 22 h.
  4. Viable only if that catch-up time is acceptable and the engine processes much faster than the live rate; if history is TB+ and replay takes days, keep Lambda.
AnswerAbout 22 h to catch up; Kappa is viable if that window is acceptable.
Practice · 3
A bank keeps 30 days of events at 50,000 events/s. Given: events to replay = rate x seconds. How many events?
Variant 1
50,000 x 30 x 86,400 = 129,600,000,000.
The bank's stream engine replays at 1 M events/s while live traffic is 50,000/s. Catch-up time for those events?
Variant 2
129,600,000,000 / 950,000 = 136,421 s = 37.9 h.
Name conditions where Kappa is not suitable.
Why
When reprocessing TB+ of history is too slow for the stream engine; when teams prefer batch SQL (Hive, Spark batch) over stream SQL; when a regulator requires a separate batch reconciliation (e.g. Bangladesh Bank end-of-day reconciliation, or DGHS audited health reports).
