  1. i)
    Social media posts: 7-10 days before ER visits. Pharmacy OTC antipyretic sales: 3-5 days before clinical confirmation. (ER chief complaints via NLP and search volume are also on the slide.)
  2. ii)
    GFT over-predicted flu by about 2x in 2012-13. Lazer et al. gave three causes: big data hubris (r = 0.97 on the training years did not generalise), algorithm confounding (Google's autocomplete changes shifted the search features), and media amplification (flu news drove searches even when incidence was low). Searches are a proxy for health anxiety, not incidence. Lesson: syndromic data gives early signals that supplement, not replace, clinical surveillance.
  3. iii)
    Spike ratio = current / baseline = 12,000 / 40 = 300x. Yes: trending is judged against the phrase's own baseline, not absolute volume.
  4. iv)
    Any two: de-identification (safe harbour: remove the 18 HIPAA identifiers such as name, NID, phone); differential privacy (calibrated noise on aggregate counts); federated learning (train at each hospital without moving raw records); explicit consent for NID-linked data under PDPA.
Prediction · not the real paper

Predicted Paper B (hedge: W10 promoted to a main question; W7 and W9 as ORs)

Built from how much the slides stress each chapter; the reasoning is shown on every question. The real paper can pick any chapter, so the plan and the pool still cover all six weeks.

Question 1Week 5 · 10 marks
Why predicted: Covers the W5 material Paper A skips: the Hadoop 1 limits, LinkedIn's case numbers (45% -> 78%) and the bKash format strategy (Avro -> Parquet+Snappy -> ORC+Zstd, 60% smaller).
(a)5 marks · tap for answers
Before YARN, LinkedIn ran three separate clusters: MapReduce for Hive ETL, an experimental Spark cluster and Samza stream nodes. In 2013 it merged them into one 5,000-node YARN cluster with the Capacity Scheduler.
  1. i)
    Why couldn't the Hadoop 1.x cluster simply run Spark and Samza too? (1)
  2. ii)
    Give the role of each YARN component in one line. (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Average utilisation rose from 45% to 78%. How much more workload does the same hardware now serve? (1)
  4. iv)
    LinkedIn turned on pre-emption. What does it do, and what went wrong at first? (1.5)
  1. i)
    The JobTracker bundled resource management with MapReduce-specific scheduling, so only MapReduce jobs could get cluster resources; it was also a single bottleneck with a ceiling of about 4,000 nodes.
  2. ii)
    ResourceManager: one per cluster, schedules containers globally (Scheduler + ApplicationsManager). NodeManager: one per node, launches and monitors containers and heartbeats to the RM. ApplicationMaster: one per application, requests containers from the RM and tells NMs which tasks to run.
  3. iii)
    78 / 45 = 1.733, so about 73% more workload on the same capacity.
  4. iv)
    Pre-emption lets a queue borrow idle capacity from other queues and takes it back when the owner needs it. Aggressive pre-emption killed long-running Spark jobs, so LinkedIn added a 30-second grace period and checkpoint-on-preempt hooks.
(b)5 marks · tap for answers
bKash's data lake ingests Kafka events as Avro, converts them nightly to Parquet+Snappy partitioned by dt= and region=, and moves data older than 2 years to ORC+Zstd. The old system kept everything as gzip CSV.
  1. i)
    Why Avro at the ingest layer? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    What do Parquet+Snappy and the dt=/region= layout give the analytics layer? (1)
  3. iii)
    50 TB of cold CSV moves to ORC+Zstd, which the slide says is 60% smaller. How much storage remains? (1)
  4. iv)
    Why was the old gzip CSV a problem for MapReduce/Hive jobs? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Avro is a self-describing row format with schema evolution: the reader-schema / writer-schema protocol gives backward and forward compatibility, so when the API adds a field old readers do not break (missing fields take defaults, extra fields are ignored). Row format also suits appending events.
  2. ii)
    Columnar reads of only the needed columns, predicate pushdown from row-group statistics, splittable files (Snappy inside row groups), and partition pruning on date and region.
  3. iii)
    50 TB x (1 - 0.60) = 20 TB.
  4. iv)
    Gzip is not splittable: MapReduce cannot start reading in the middle of a gzip stream, so each file, however large, goes to exactly one Mapper (a 10 GB file = 1 Mapper). Use Parquet+Snappy or bzip2 instead.
Question 2Week 6 · 10 marks
Why predicted: Covers the remaining slide examples: filter(x>1000).first() (pool D3), the 10 iterations over 100 GB 'about 3 hours' number (P2 s4), and GraySort (P2 s14-15, 32x per node in Key Takeaways).
(a)4 marks · tap for answers
An analyst runs rdd.filter(lambda x: x > 1000).first() on a 1 TB dataset and is surprised it returns in seconds. A colleague says the same 10-iteration job over 100 GB on MapReduce spent about 3 hours on disk I/O.
  1. i)
    What is lazy evaluation? (1)
  2. ii)
    Why does first() return so quickly here? (1)
  3. iii)
    Check the colleague's figure: 10 iterations over 100 GB at 100 MB/s. (1)
  4. iv)
    Name two transformations and two actions. (1)
  1. i)
    Transformations such as filter and map only record a step in the DAG and return a new RDD; nothing executes until an action (count, collect, first, saveAsTextFile) is called.
  2. ii)
    When first() triggers the DAG, Spark pipelines the filter and stops as soon as it finds the first matching element; it never filters the whole 1 TB. Without lazy evaluation the full filter would run first.
  3. iii)
    Reads only: 10 x 100 GB = 1,000 GB = 1,000,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 10,000 s = about 2.8 h, the slide's 'about 3 hours'. Counting the writes too doubles it to 20,000 s = about 5.6 h.
  4. iv)
    Transformations: map, filter (also flatMap, reduceByKey, join, groupByKey, distinct). Actions: count, collect (also first, take(n), reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach).
(b)6 marks · tap for answers
In November 2013 Databricks sorted 100 TB in 23 minutes on 206 EC2 nodes. The previous Hadoop record was 72 minutes on 2,100 nodes. The sort is a single sortByKey.
  1. i)
    Why is the shuffle the bottleneck of a distributed sort, and what did Spark change in it? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    Spark was 3.1x faster on 10.2x fewer nodes. What is its efficiency per node relative to Hadoop? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Define narrow and wide dependencies with one example each, and say how each affects stages. (1.5)
  4. iv)
    Why should a word count use reduceByKey rather than groupByKey? (1.5)
  1. i)
    Every record crosses the network between map and reduce sides, and MapReduce's shuffle spills, merges and re-reads intermediate data on disk many times (about 200 TB of extra I/O at 100 TB). Spark used a sort-based shuffle that writes sorted runs once and then merges, spread over 8 SSDs per node, with off-heap sort buffers that avoid GC pauses.
  2. ii)
    Per-node efficiency = 3.1 x 10.2 = about 31.6, about 32x (72/23 = 3.13 and 2,100/206 = 10.19 give 31.9).
  3. iii)
    Narrow: each output partition depends on at most one input partition (map, filter, union); no shuffle, pipelined in one stage. Wide: an output partition depends on many input partitions (groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, sortByKey); needs a shuffle and starts a new stage.
  4. iv)
    reduceByKey combines values locally on each partition before the shuffle (like a MapReduce Combiner), so only one partial sum per key per partition crosses the network. groupByKey ships every (word, 1) pair, so it moves far more data.
OR
(a (OR)) W74 marks · tap for answers
By 2008 Facebook had hundreds of analysts who knew SQL but not Java. Today a ministry wants district-wise counts from a 30-million-row health table: SELECT district, COUNT(*) FROM visits GROUP BY district (64 districts).
  1. i)
    What problem did Hive solve? (1)
  2. ii)
    What do HiveServer2 and the Driver do? (1)
  3. iii)
    With map-side aggregation each mapper emits partial counts per district instead of one row per record. By what factor does the shuffle shrink (treat it as one mapper)? (1)
  4. iv)
    Why do production teams run the Metastore as a highly available service? (1)
  1. i)
    Every query used to be a Java MapReduce program (100+ lines for a GROUP BY, days to insight). Hive lets analysts write declarative SQL-like HiveQL, which Hive compiles into MapReduce, Tez or Spark jobs.
  2. ii)
    HiveServer2 is the JDBC/ODBC server that authenticates users and accepts queries from Beeline and BI tools. The Driver runs the pipeline: parser -> semantic analyser -> logical planner -> optimiser -> physical plan, and submits the jobs.
  3. iii)
    30,000,000 rows / 64 partial counts = 468,750x less shuffle data.
  4. iv)
    Without it Hive cannot find where any table lives or how to parse it, so Metastore corruption means no table can be queried even though the HDFS data is intact.
(b (OR)) W76 marks · tap for answers
Table play_events is partitioned by dt (30 days kept) and country (50 countries). A dashboard asks for plays on dt='2024-10-01' in BD and IN. It takes 6 minutes on Hive+MapReduce; Presto does it in seconds.
  1. i)
    List the compiler steps Hive goes through for this query. (1.5)
  2. ii)
    What fraction of partitions does the query read? (1)
  3. iii)
    Give the design decisions that make Presto faster for this dashboard. (2)
  4. iv)
    Give one advantage and one risk of Hive's schema-on-read. (1.5)
  1. i)
    Parse HiveQL into an AST -> semantic analysis (resolve columns and types against the Metastore, note dt and country are partition columns) -> logical plan (filter, aggregate) -> physical plan of MR/Tez jobs with partition pruning -> submit to YARN.
  2. ii)
    Total = 30 x 50 = 1,500 partitions; it reads 2, so 2 / 1,500 = about 0.13%; 1,498 are skipped.
  3. iii)
    No intermediate disk writes: data flows as an in-memory pipeline (Hive+MR writes to HDFS between stages). Vectorised execution over batches of 1,024 rows. Cost-based optimiser using table statistics for join order and strategy. Connector architecture: one SQL engine over HDFS/Hive, Cassandra, MySQL, Kafka, S3.
  4. iv)
    Advantage: raw files load fast with no ETL at ingest, and several tables (schemas) can be defined over the same files as needs change. Risk: data-quality problems stay silent until query time; a corrupt value comes back as NULL instead of an error, so pipelines need separate validation.
Question 3Week 10 · 10 marks
Why predicted: W10 is CLO4 (problem solving), is the last chapter taught, and has two papers plus a case study. Promoted to a main question here as the hedge against Paper A's ranking. Uses VADER thresholds, Louvain steps, Prophet terms and the STL k x IQR rule.
(a)4 marks · tap for answers
A research group tracks Bangla and English posts on X during an election week. They score posts with VADER and look for groups of accounts that retweet each other heavily.
  1. i)
    Why use VADER rather than a generic sentiment model? Give two features it handles. (1)
  2. ii)
    Three posts score compound 0.31, -0.02 and -0.47. Classify each. (1)
  3. iii)
    Give the steps of the Louvain algorithm. (1)
  4. iv)
    Give one ethical risk of this analysis. (1)
  1. i)
    VADER is a lexicon-and-rule analyser tuned for social media. Any two: capitalisation (GREAT > great), punctuation (great!!!), degree modifiers (very good), negation (not good), emojis.
  2. ii)
    Positive if > 0.05, negative if < -0.05, else neutral: 0.31 positive, -0.02 neutral, -0.47 negative.
  3. iii)
    Start with each node as its own community; greedily move each node into the neighbouring community that most increases modularity; aggregate communities into super-nodes and repeat; stop when modularity no longer increases. About O(n log n).
  4. iv)
    Sentiment scoring of political speech can be used to suppress dissent (flag negative posts about the government) or to micro-target vulnerable users; needs transparency and purpose limitation.
(b)6 marks · tap for answers
A hospital group forecasts weekly admissions with Prophet and also flags unusual weeks. Its model has strong yearly and weekly seasonality but missed the sudden onset of a COVID-19 wave. The residuals after STL decomposition have IQR = 4.
  1. i)
    Write Prophet's model and name each term. (1.5)
  2. ii)
    What do p, d and q mean in ARIMA, and why is ARIMA a weak fit here? (1.5)
  3. iii)
    Flag residuals beyond k x IQR with k = 3. Weeks have residuals 15 and -9. Which is an anomaly? (1)
  4. iv)
    Which Prophet component should catch the COVID wave, which hyperparameter controls it, and how does Isolation Forest find anomalies? (2)
  1. i)
    y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t): g = trend (piecewise linear or logistic, with changepoints), s = seasonality (Fourier series, yearly/weekly), h = holidays and events (e.g. Eid), e = residual noise.
  2. ii)
    AR(p): depends on the past p values; I(d): difference d times to make the series stationary; MA(q): depends on the past q forecast errors. ARIMA assumes stationarity, handles multiple seasonalities poorly and needs manual (p, d, q) choice per series.
  3. iii)
    Threshold = 3 x 4 = 12. |15| > 12, so that week is an anomaly; |-9| = 9 < 12, so it is not.
  4. iv)
    The trend g(t) through its changepoints. changepoint_prior_scale sets the sparse prior on the slope changes: raising it (e.g. 0.05 -> 0.5) makes the trend more flexible. Isolation Forest builds random trees that partition the data; anomalies need fewer splits to isolate, so they have shorter average path lengths.
Question 4Week 8 · 10 marks
Why predicted: Pool A1 (bank pipeline) is the W8 design question; the Kafka paper's benchmark table gives a ready calculation (50.5 MB/s at 100 B = 505,000 msg/s).
(a)5 marks · tap for answers
A commercial bank must (1) copy 10 million customer records from Oracle to Hadoop every night, (2) decide on card-swipe fraud within 200 ms, and (3) keep a risk dashboard no more than 5 minutes old.
  1. i)
    Which tool handles (1), and how does it work inside? (1.5)
  2. ii)
    Which tools handle (2)? (1)
  3. iii)
    The nightly import runs with 4 map tasks splitting on customer_id. How many rows does each read if keys are evenly spread? (1)
  4. iv)
    Lambda or Kappa for the whole system? Justify. (1.5)
  1. i)
    Apache Sqoop. sqoop import launches a MapReduce job whose map tasks each read a primary-key range of the table in parallel over JDBC and write to HDFS (Parquet/Avro/CSV) or Hive. Incremental import with check-column and last-value copies only new rows.
  2. ii)
    Kafka carries the swipe events; Spark Streaming (or Flink) consumes them and scores each event within the 200 ms budget. Sqoop is batch and Flume is for logs, so neither fits.
  3. iii)
    10,000,000 / 4 = 2,500,000 rows per map task.
  4. iv)
    Lambda fits: there is a genuine nightly batch (Sqoop + Hive/Spark for accurate risk reports, regulatory reconciliation) beside a low-latency stream for fraud and the dashboard. Kappa would suit if a single stream engine could also replay the full history fast enough, but a regulator-mandated batch reconciliation is one of the slide's 'Kappa not suitable' cases.
(b)5 marks · tap for answers
In 2010 LinkedIn found ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ could not carry billions of activity events a day. In the Kafka paper's benchmark (one broker, 100-byte messages) the producer throughputs were ActiveMQ 4.3 MB/s, RabbitMQ 14.7 MB/s, Kafka 50.5 MB/s.
  1. i)
    Explain the two storage decisions behind Kafka's speed. (2)
  2. ii)
    How many messages per second is Kafka's 50.5 MB/s, and how many times ActiveMQ's throughput? (1)
  3. iii)
    What does 'consumer pull' mean, and why does it help the broker? (1)
  4. iv)
    The bank later dumps every raw file into S3 with no catalogue or owners. What does the lake become, and give one prevention step. (1)
  1. i)
    Sequential writes: Kafka only appends to segment files, so disks run at sequential speed (about 600 MB/s vs about 100 MB/s random), helped by the OS page cache. Zero-copy: sendfile() sends data from the kernel page cache straight to the NIC, cutting 4 copies to 2 and skipping user space, so CPU stays near zero.
  2. ii)
    50.5 MB/s / 100 B = 50,500,000 / 100 = 505,000 messages/s. 50.5 / 4.3 = about 11.7x ActiveMQ.
  3. iii)
    Consumers fetch data and track their own offsets (stored in __consumer_offsets); the broker keeps no per-consumer queues or per-message ACKs, so one log serves any number of consumers cheaply.
  4. iv)
    A data swamp: nobody can find datasets or tell current from stale copies, and PII is mixed in. Prevention: enforce a data catalogue at ingest (Hive Metastore/Glue/Atlas), with owners, access control, quality checks or a table format like Delta/Iceberg.
OR
(a (OR)) W95 marks · tap for answers
An analyst reports that four regional sales datasets have the same mean, variance and correlation (r = 0.816), so 'they behave the same'. Another report shows revenue up 5%, but the bar is drawn 40% taller because the y-axis does not start at 0.
  1. i)
    What does Anscombe's quartet say about the analyst's conclusion? (1)
  2. ii)
    A manager wants the share of revenue from 9 product lines. Is a pie chart right? What should be used? (1)
  3. iii)
    Compute the lie factor of the revenue chart and say what it means. (1)
  4. iv)
    Define small multiples and sparklines, with one use each. (2)
  1. i)
    Four datasets with identical summary statistics look completely different when plotted (linear, curved, one outlier, a vertical cluster). Plot the data before trusting the statistics.
  2. ii)
    No. Pies only suit 4 or fewer categories and a 'fraction of the whole' question; people judge angles poorly. Use a horizontal bar chart.
  3. iii)
    Lie factor = effect shown / effect in data = 40% / 5% = 8. Above 1, so the chart overstates the change eightfold.
  4. iv)
    Small multiples: the same chart structure repeated for each subset (district, year) on the same scale, for side-by-side comparison, e.g. a 50-state grid of case curves. Sparklines: word-sized line charts embedded in text or table cells, adding trend context, e.g. a tiny 7-day trend beside each district's case count.
(b (OR)) W95 marks · tap for answers
bKash fraud operations want a live chart of transaction volume. Events arrive in Kafka at 3,000 transactions per second, are aggregated by Spark Structured Streaming in 1-minute tumbling windows, stored in a time-series DB and shown in Grafana with a 5-second refresh. A second screen plots millions of transactions as a scatter.
  1. i)
    Describe the four-step streaming visualisation architecture. (1.5)
  2. ii)
    How many transactions does each 1-minute window summarise? (1)
  3. iii)
    When would you push updates over WebSocket instead of Grafana's polling? (1)
  4. iv)
    The scatter is a solid blob. Give three fixes in increasing sophistication. (1.5)
  1. i)
    1) Events arrive in a Kafka topic. 2) Spark Structured Streaming or Flink aggregates them over a window. 3) Results are written to a time-series DB (InfluxDB, Prometheus, Elasticsearch). 4) Grafana or Kibana polls the DB every few seconds and redraws.
  2. ii)
    3,000 x 60 = 180,000 transactions per window.
  3. iii)
    When sub-second updates are needed (stock tickers, live election counts): the server pushes each update and a D3.js chart re-renders on every push. Polling every 5 s is enough for ops dashboards.
  4. iv)
    Alpha transparency (e.g. 0.02, denser areas darker, fails at extreme density); hexbin aggregation (count per hexagon, about 10 M points -> about 10,000 cells); KDE / 2-D density contours (shows shape, modes and tails).
Last ten minutes

Must-know and formula sheet

The must-know list first, then every formula from weeks 5–10. The one-line answer for each topic sits at the top of its card; flash all 36 below.

Must-know: 40 lines tick each one you can say from memory

  • YARN: RM = one per cluster (Scheduler + ApplicationsManager); NM = one per node (containers, heartbeat); AM = one per application (requests containers). Hadoop 2.0 (2013) replaced the JobTracker (MR only, ~4,000 nodes).
  • Container = {vCPU, RAM} slice on one node; NM kills a container that exceeds its memory limit.
  • YARN failures: NM -> missed heartbeat, containers marked failed, AM re-requests; AM -> RM restarts it (max attempts, default 2); RM -> HA with ZooKeeper (active + standby).
  • Schedulers: FIFO (starves), Capacity (guaranteed queue %, borrows idle capacity), Fair (equal shares, short jobs finish fast). DRF = fairness over CPU and RAM.
  • Containers per queue = min(queue RAM / container RAM, queue vCPU / container vCPU); the smaller one is the bottleneck.
  • Columnar: read = D x k/N; 10 TB, 3 of 100 columns -> 300 GB, 97% less, ~33x.
  • Parquet: row groups (~128 MB) -> column chunks -> pages; footer min/max stats -> predicate pushdown skips row groups.
  • Avro = row, schema evolution (reader/writer schema), Kafka ingest. Parquet = columnar, Spark analytics. ORC = columnar, Hive, highest compression.
  • Gzip is NOT splittable (1 Mapper per file). Bzip2 splittable; LZO splittable with index; Snappy fast (splittable inside Parquet row groups).
  • Spark beats MR on iteration: MR = k x (read + write) on HDFS; Spark reads once and caches. 50 GB x 100 iterations: 10 TB vs 50 GB.
  • Spark architecture: Driver (SparkContext/SparkSession, builds DAG) -> Cluster Manager (YARN/K8s/Mesos/Standalone) -> Executors (tasks + cache).
  • RDD = read-only, partitioned collection created from stable storage or other RDDs; immutable, partitioned, lazy, lineage, resilient (recompute, not replicate).
  • Transformations (lazy): map, filter, flatMap, reduceByKey, groupByKey, join, distinct. Actions: count, collect, first, take, reduce, saveAsTextFile, foreach.
  • Lazy evaluation lets Spark pipeline narrow steps and stop early: filter(x > 1000).first().
  • Narrow (1 parent partition, same stage): map, filter, union, coalesce. Wide (shuffle, new stage): groupByKey, reduceByKey, join, repartition, distinct, sortByKey.
  • reduceByKey > groupByKey: it combines locally before the shuffle. Hash partitioner = key.hashCode() % numPartitions.
  • DataFrame = named columns + schema, Catalyst optimiser. HBase is NOT part of the Spark ecosystem.
  • Hive: HiveServer2 (JDBC/ODBC) -> Driver (parse -> semantic -> logical -> optimise -> physical) -> engine MR/Tez/Spark; Metastore (MySQL/PostgreSQL) holds schemas, partitions + HDFS paths, SerDe, stats.
  • Schema-on-read (Hive): schema applied at query, bad value -> NULL, fast load. Schema-on-write (RDBMS): rejected at INSERT. HiveQL: limited ACID (ORC transactional only), minutes of latency.
  • Partitioning = HDFS sub-directory per value, prunes scans; low-cardinality columns only (user_id -> partition explosion). Dynamic insert: partition columns last in SELECT.
  • Bucketing = hash(col) % N files; bucket map join (same key, same N) avoids a shuffle. Fraction read = partitions read / total.
  • Map-side aggregation: 50 M rows, 200 countries -> 250,000x less shuffle.
  • Presto: in-memory pipeline (no intermediate disk), vectorised 1,024-row batches, cost-based optimiser, connectors.
  • Point-to-point ETL = N(N-1) jobs (50 -> 2,450); bus = N connections.
  • Sqoop = bulk RDBMS <-> HDFS via a MapReduce job whose map tasks each read a primary-key range, incremental last-value. Flume = Source -> Channel (memory/file) -> Sink, logs to HDFS.
  • Kafka = distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Topic -> partitions (ordered, same key -> same partition) -> offsets; consumer tracks its own offset; retention (e.g. 7 days) -> replay from offset 0.
  • RF = R survives R - 1 broker failures; one leader + R - 1 followers. In a consumer group, each partition goes to exactly one consumer (extra consumers idle).
  • Kafka speed: sequential appends (~600 vs ~100 MB/s), zero-copy sendfile (4 -> 2 copies), batching, consumer pull. 50.5 MB/s / 100 B = 505,000 msg/s.
  • Lambda (Marz): Batch (HDFS, accurate, hours) + Speed (stream, seconds, approximate) + Serving (merge). Weakness: two code paths (30-40% effort).
  • Kappa (Kreps): one stream code path over a durable log; reprocess = new job from offset 0, catch up, swap. Not for very slow TB-scale replay, batch-SQL preference, or mandated batch reconciliation.
  • Data lake = raw data, any format, schema-on-read; layers: ingestion, storage, processing, catalogue/governance. No governance -> data swamp.
  • Tufte: data-ink ratio = data ink / total ink (maximise); chartjunk (3-D, gradients, heavy grids, ducks); small multiples; sparklines; lie factor = effect shown / effect in data (1 = truthful).
  • Shneiderman: 'Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand'; 7 data types: 1-D, 2-D, 3-D, temporal, multi-dimensional, tree, network.
  • Chart choice: temporal -> line; categories -> bar (pie only if 4 or fewer and part-of-whole); geography -> choropleth; distribution -> histogram/box; correlation -> scatter.
  • Big-data viz challenges: overplotting (alpha -> hexbin -> KDE), latency (data cube / AQP, trade-off staleness), streaming (Kafka -> Spark window -> TSDB -> Grafana poll / WebSocket push).
  • Tools: Grafana = real-time ops; Tableau/Power BI = business BI; D3.js = custom web SVG; Superset = open-source BI on lakes; Kibana = Elasticsearch logs.
  • Time series: order matters, autocorrelation, trend, seasonality, non-stationarity. ARIMA(p, d, q) = AR lags, differencing, MA errors; needs stationarity and manual tuning.
  • Prophet: y = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + e(t); changepoints in g (changepoint_prior_scale); Fourier seasonality; holidays; scale with groupBy + applyInPandas.
  • Social: Louvain maximises modularity (merge, aggregate, repeat); influence maximisation NP-hard, greedy (1 - 1/e); Kwak: 22.1% reciprocity, 4.12 hops, power law -> Twitter is a news medium. VADER: > 0.05 positive, < -0.05 negative.
  • Health: EHR, genomics (~200 GB/genome), wearables, DICOM (unstructured); HIPAA 18 identifiers, GDPR, PDPA; DP and federated learning. GFT over-predicted 2x: syndromic data supplements, never replaces.

Low-yield detail by the slide evidence. Skip only if the clock forces it; everything else stays in.

  • Paper citations, author lists, venues, citation counts and timelines (Vavilapalli, Zaharia, Thusoo, Kreps, Tufte, Shneiderman, Kwak, Taylor & Letham): know the idea each paper introduced, not the bibliography.
  • Company scale trivia not used by any pool question: Spotify 1 M tables / 600 B events, Netflix 4,000 topics / 2,000 brokers, Facebook 7,500 queries/day, LinkedIn 30,000 jobs/day, NYT 6 M readers.
  • Python/D3/PySpark live-exercise skeleton code line by line (know what each exercise demonstrates, not the syntax).
  • Spotify Discover Weekly details (Word2Vec, Annoy, CNN audio embeddings, Luigi) and the ALS model-size discussion.
  • W6 P2 persistence levels beyond MEMORY_ONLY vs MEMORY_AND_DISK; GraySort hardware specs (i2.8xlarge, SSD totals).
  • Hive 2010 paper extras: compact/bitmap indexes, LLAP, Iceberg REST catalog, AWS Glue; Kafka extras: ksqlDB, tiered storage, Schema Registry details.
  • Netflix A/B-testing pipeline step list; Timeline Server REST details; DRF maths.
  • AlphaFold architecture details (Evoformer, GDT score, TPU counts): know only 'protein 3D structure from sequence, trained on PDB, MSA over 250 M sequences'.
  • Prophet trend and Fourier formulas written out symbol by symbol (know g/s/h/e meanings and changepoint_prior_scale).
  • University-curricula slides (Harvard CS171, Stanford CS246, CMU 15-721, MIT 6.830) and quote-of-the-week slides.

Week 5 YARN, file formats and compression · 7

Columnar data read
Read = D × k / N
D table size, k columns selected, N total columns
Columnar I/O reduction
Reduction = 1 − k / N; speedup ≈ N / k
10 TB, 3 of 100: 97%, 33×
Pushdown saving
Speedup = D / R
R = bytes actually read; 10 TB / 50 GB = 200×
Mappers per file
Splits = ⌈F / B⌉, or 1 if gzip
B = block or row group, about 128 MB
Containers per queue
min(nodes·f·RAM / c_ram, nodes·f·CPU / c_cpu)
smaller term is the bottleneck
Nodes for a job
⌈T / min(RAM / c_ram, CPU / c_cpu)⌉
T containers needed at once
Extra work from utilisation
U_new / U_old − 1
78/45 − 1 = 73%

Week 6 Apache Spark: RDDs and in-memory computing · 8

MapReduce iterative disk I/O
MR_IO = k × (D_read + D_write)
k iterations; slide: 100 × (50 + 50) GB = 10 TB
Spark HDFS I/O
Spark_IO = D (read once)
later iterations read RAM, not HDFS
Transfer time
t = size / speed
50,000 MB / 500 MB/s = 100 s
Iterative wall-clock time
T_MR = k × (D/R_hdfs + D/W_hdfs); T_Spark = D/R_hdfs + (k − 1) × D/R_ram
k − 1 RAM passes, not k
Speedup
Speedup = T_old / T_new
A1: 20,000 / 1,090 ≈ 18.3×; RDD paper 127 / 0.96 ≈ 132×
Hash partitioner
partition = key.hashCode() % numPartitions
17 % 4 = 1
Shuffle records
groupByKey = all pairs; reduceByKey ≤ partitions × distinct keys per partition
4,000 vs 200 records
Efficiency per node
(T_old × N_old) / (T_new × N_new)
GraySort (72 × 2,100) / (23 × 206) ≈ 32×

Week 7 Hive, HiveQL and SQL-on-Hadoop · 7

Map-side aggregation
reduction = N_rows / G (with M mappers: N_rows / (M × G))
50M rows, 200 countries: 250,000×
Partition pruning
fraction read = P_read / P_total
P_total = product of values per partition column
Bucket number
bucket = hash(column) % N
integer key: hash = value; 98 % 4 = 2
Bucket file size
size = S / (P × N); files = P × N
aim near the 128 MB HDFS block
ALS model size
(users + items) × k × bytes
(75M + 30M) × 50 × 4 B = 21 GB
Speed-up
T_old / T_new; saved = (T_old − T_new) / T_old
8 h to 2 h: 4×, 75% saved
Pairs in a playlist
L(L − 1) / 2
20 songs: 190 pairs

Week 8 Data integration: Kafka, Lambda/Kappa, data lakes · 9

Point-to-point ETL jobs
N × (N − 1); bus = N
50 systems: 2,450 jobs vs 50 connections
Partition copies
P × R
bkash-txns: 3 × 2 = 6
Broker failures survived
R − 1
default R = 3 survives 2
Active consumers in a group
min(P, C); idle = C − P (only if C > P)
one consumer per partition per group
Messages per second
MB/s × 1,000,000 ÷ message bytes
50.5 MB/s, 100 B = 505,000 msgs/s
Speedup
Kafka ÷ other
50.5 / 4.3 ≈ 11.7×; 50.5 / 14.7 ≈ 3.4×
Sequential vs random disk
seq ÷ random
600 / 100 = 6× (paper figures)
Zero-copy
4 copies → 2 copies
about 2× throughput, CPU near zero
Events per second
events per day ÷ 86,400
Netflix 100 B/day ≈ 1.16 M/s

Week 9 Data visualization · 8

Data-ink ratio
ink encoding data ÷ total ink
Maximise it; 1 is the ceiling
Lie factor
effect shown in graphic ÷ effect in data
1 truthful; above 1 overstates; below 1 understates
Hexbin reduction
points ÷ hex cells
10 M ÷ 10,000 = 1,000×
Alpha stacking
opacity = 1 − (1 − α)ⁿ
α = 0.02: n = 100 → 0.867, saturates
Cube rows
≤ d₁ × d₂ × … × dₖ; reduction = fact rows ÷ cube rows
100 B ÷ 5 M = 20,000×
Group-by combinations
2ᵏ for k dimensions
k = 4 → 16
Events per window
rate × window seconds
10,000/s × 60 = 600,000
Updates per day
86,400 ÷ refresh seconds
Every 5 min → 288

Week 10 Big data in real applications · 13

Prophet model
y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε(t)
trend + seasonality + holidays + noise
Prophet trend
g(t) = (k + a(t)ᵀδ) t + (m + a(t)ᵀγ)
δ slope changes at changepoints, sparse prior
Fourier seasonality
s(t) = Σ [aₙ cos(2πnt/P) + bₙ sin(2πnt/P)], n = 1..N
P = 365.25 yearly, 7 weekly
ARIMA(p, d, q)
AR past p values; I difference d times; MA past q errors
needs stationary input
Speedup
T_sequential / T_parallel
480 min / 12 min = 40× (5,000 SKUs)
Reach in h hops
d + d² + … + d^h
upper bound; d = 45, h = 3 gives 93,195
Greedy influence bound
spread ≥ (1 − 1/e) × optimal ≈ 0.632 × optimal
Kempe et al. 2003
Modularity (words)
fraction of edges inside communities − fraction expected by chance
Louvain maximises it
Power law
P(k) ∝ k^(−α), α ≈ 2.276
Twitter follower counts (Kwak 2010)
Spike ratio
current rate / baseline rate
10 to 10,000 per hour = 1,000×
VADER classes
> 0.05 positive; < −0.05 negative; else neutral
compound in [−1, +1]
STL anomaly rule
|residual| > k × IQR, IQR = Q3 − Q1
IQR of residuals, not raw data
Genomics storage
200 GB × patients (× replication)
10,000 patients = 2 PB
